docs.text:
• Tanenbaum §5.1–§5.4.
  • Silberschatz §13.1–§13.5.

docs.title: Chapter 9 — Introduction to Security
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Coverage: threats and attacks · defences.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
1. Classify security threats: malware (virus, worm, trojan), buffer overflow, DoS, social engineering.
  2. Describe authentication mechanisms (passwords, biometrics, multi-factor).
  3. Explain access control (ACLs, capabilities, mandatory vs. discretionary).
  4. Describe defences: sandboxing, ASLR, DEP, firewalls, encryption.

docs.title: 9.1.1 Malware
docs.text:
Type Description Propagation Virus Attaches to a host program Requires user action to spread Worm Standalone program Self-propagates over the network Trojan Malicious code disguised as legitimate software User installs it voluntarily

Why worms are more dangerous

A worm propagates automatically over the network, exploiting vulnerabilities without any user action. A virus requires the user to run an infected program, so its spread is slower and more limited.

docs.title: 9.1.2 Buffer overflow
docs.text:
A buffer overflow occurs when a program writes more data into a buffer than it can hold, overwriting adjacent memory (including the return address on the stack).

Classic attack: overwrite the return address to jump to shellcode placed earlier in the buffer.

Defences:

  • Bounds checking at compile time (safe languages).
  • Stack canaries — a random value placed between the buffer and the return address; if it changes, the program aborts.
  • ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomisation) — randomise stack, heap, and library addresses so the attacker cannot predict where to jump.
  • DEP / NX (Data Execution Prevention / No-eXecute) — mark stack and heap as non-executable.

docs.title: 9.1.3 Denial of Service (DoS)
docs.text:
An attacker floods a service with requests until it can no longer respond to legitimate users. Distributed DoS (DDoS) uses a botnet of compromised machines.

Defences: rate limiting, traffic filtering, anycast distribution, CAPTCHAs.

docs.title: 9.1.4 Social engineering
docs.text: Manipulating people into revealing confidential information or performing actions that compromise security. Phishing, pretexting, baiting.

docs.title: 9.2 Authentication
docs.text:
Authentication verifies who you are. Three factors:

Factor Example Something you know Password, PIN Something you have Smart card, hardware token, phone Something you are Fingerprint, face recognition, iris scan

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) combines two or more factors — e.g., password + one-time code from a phone.

Password storage. Passwords must never be stored in plaintext. Use:

  • Salted hash — a random salt per user, then a slow hash (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2).
  • Never MD5 or SHA-1 for passwords — they are too fast and broken.

docs.title: 9.3 Authorisation and access control
docs.text:
Authorisation determines what you can do.

Model Description Discretionary access control (DAC) Owner decides who gets access (Unix permissions, ACLs) Mandatory access control (MAC) System-wide policy decides (SELinux, AppArmor) Role-based access control (RBAC) Permissions assigned to roles, not individuals

Unix permissions are a simple DAC scheme: each file has an owner, group, and mode bits (read / write / execute for owner, group, others).

docs.title: 9.4 Defences
docs.text:
• Principle of least privilege — every component should have only the permissions it needs.
  • Sandboxing — run untrusted code in an isolated environment (browser tabs, containers).
  • Encryption — at rest (disk encryption) and in transit (TLS).
  • Firewalls — filter network traffic by port, source, or protocol.
  • Intrusion detection / prevention systems (IDS/IPS) — monitor for known attack patterns.
  • Security updates — patch known vulnerabilities promptly.
  • Audit logging — record security-relevant events for post-incident analysis.

docs.title: 9.5 Quiz
docs.text:
1. Compare viruses, worms, and trojans on propagation.
  2. Explain the buffer-overflow attack and three defences.
  3. What is the difference between authentication and authorisation?
  4. Why must passwords be stored as salted hashes, not plaintext?
  5. Describe the principle of least privilege and give one example.

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
Click to reveal
  1. Virus: needs a host, requires user action. Worm: standalone, self-propagates over the network. Trojan: disguised as legitimate software, user installs it.
  2. Overflow a buffer, overwrite the return address, jump to shellcode. Defences: stack canaries, ASLR, DEP.
  3. Authentication verifies identity; authorisation determines permissions.
  4. Salted hashes prevent rainbow-table attacks and hide identical passwords; slow hashes resist brute force.
  5. Every component should have only the privileges it needs. Example: a web server runs as an unprivileged user, not root.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Tanenbaum §9.1–§9.5.
  • Silberschatz §15.1–§15.4.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text: 1. Define what an **operating system** is, and why it exists.     2. Trace the **evolution** of OS from batch to mobile, and identify what changed at each step.     3. Compare **monolithic**, **layered**, **microkernel**, **modular**, and **hybrid** OS structures.     4. Describe the **computer system organisation** (CPU, memory, I/O, buses) and the role of **interrupts**.     5. Explain **dual-mode operation** and its role in OS protection.     6. Trace a **system call** from user space to kernel and back.

docs.title: 1.1 — What is an Operating System?
docs.text:
Definition (Tanenbaum §1.1)

An operating system is a program that acts as an intermediary between the user and the computer hardware. Its primary goals are convenience for the user and efficient utilisation of the hardware.

???+ info "Two views" **Top-down (user's view):** the OS is the interface that makes the hardware usable — files, processes, sockets, windows. **Bottom-up (resource manager):** the OS is the allocator of CPU, memory, devices, and storage among competing processes. !!! tip "Where does the OS live?" The **kernel** is the part of the OS that runs in **privileged mode** and has direct access to hardware. User-space programs (including most of the OS "system utilities") run in **unprivileged mode** and interact with the kernel via **system calls**. Open by anchoring the two views. Students often think "OS = Windows/Ubuntu GUI" — but the GUI is just one user-space application. The OS is the kernel: the layer that mediates hardware access. Emphasise this distinction early; it will come up again in every chapter.

docs.title: 1.1 — What the OS Manages
docs.text:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                 Applications                     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│              Operating System (Kernel)           │
│  ┌──────────┬──────────┬───────────┬──────────┐ │
│  │ Process  │ Memory   │ File      │ I/O      │ │
│  │ Manager  │ Manager  │ System    │ Manager  │ │
│  └──────────┴──────────┴───────────┴──────────┘ │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                    Hardware                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
???+ note "Four resource categories" | Resource | Managed by | Chapter | |---|---|---| | **CPU** | Scheduler | 3 | | **Memory** | Memory manager | 6 | | **Storage / files** | File system | 7 | | **I/O devices** | I/O subsystem | 8 | !!! warning "The OS is not a process" The kernel is **not** a process that runs periodically. It is **invoked** on demand — by system calls, interrupts, and exceptions. Between invocations, it is dormant code sitting in memory.

docs.title: 1.2 — The OS as an Abstraction Layer
docs.text:
The layering 
User program
     │  printf()       ← libc
     ▼
System-call wrapper
     │  write(fd, buf, n)
     ▼
Kernel
     │  performs the actual I/O
     ▼
Hardware
???+ info "What abstraction buys you" - **Portability** — the same `write()` works on any disk. - **Safety** — a program cannot corrupt the disk directly. - **Simplicity** — a program does not manage DMA channels. - **Sharing** — the OS multiplexes the disk across processes. !!! tip "The three windows every OS exposes" Every OS provides at least three abstractions: 1. **Process** — a running program with its own address space. 2. **File** — a persistent, named byte stream. 3. **Socket (or pipe)** — a channel for communication.

docs.title: 1.3 — Evolution of Operating Systems
docs.text: The four generations Gen Years Hardware OS feature 0th 1940s Vacuum tubes, plugboards No OS — direct hardware control 1st 1950s Transistors, mainframes Batch monitors — automated job sequencing 2nd 1960s ICs Multiprogramming, spooling, time-sharing 3rd 1970s–80s LSI/VLSI UNIX, MS-DOS, networked OS 4th 1990s–present VLSI, mobile, cloud GUI, mobile, virtualisation, containers   ???+ note "What changed at each step"     - **Batch monitor** — eliminated the human operator between jobs.     - **Multiprogramming** — several jobs in memory; when one blocks on I/O, the CPU switches to another.     - **Time-sharing** — many interactive users; the OS switches rapidly so each user perceives the system as dedicated.     - **Virtualisation** — one physical machine runs many isolated VMs, each with its own kernel.

docs.title: 1.4 — Batch Systems
docs.text:
The batch model (1950s) 
Job 1  ──►  Memory  ──►  CPU  ──►  output
Job 2  ──►     │
Job 3  ──►     │  wait (job 1 finishes)
               ▼
          "batch" queued on tape
???+ info "The batch monitor" - Reads jobs from a **card reader or tape**. - Transfers control to the job. - When the job finishes (or crashes), control returns to the monitor. - The monitor is the first **resident** program — always in memory. !!! warning "The bottleneck" The CPU is **idle** whenever a job is doing I/O. With tape-based I/O taking seconds per byte, CPU utilisation was often < 10%.

docs.title: 1.5 — Multiprogramming and Time-Sharing
docs.text:
Multiprogramming

Multiple jobs kept in memory at once. When the running job blocks on I/O, the CPU switches to another.

Memory:
┌──────────┐
│ Job 1    │ ← running
├──────────┤
│ Job 2    │ ← ready
├──────────┤
│ Job 3    │ ← blocked on I/O
└──────────┘
???+ note "Time-sharing (multitasking)" A special case of multiprogramming where the CPU switches between jobs rapidly (every 10–100 ms) to give each **interactive user** the illusion of a dedicated machine. ???+ info "The two key mechanisms" - **Context switch** — save the state of the running process, restore the state of the next. - **Timer interrupt** — the hardware periodically forces a return to the kernel, so no process can monopolise the CPU.

docs.title: 1.6 — OS Structures: The Five Families
docs.text: How is the kernel organised internally? Structure Description Example Monolithic One big kernel; all services in one address space Traditional Linux Layered Hierarchy of layers; each uses only the one below THE OS (1968) Microkernel Only essential services in kernel; the rest in user space QNX, MINIX, seL4 Modular Monolithic core + loadable modules Linux, Solaris Hybrid Mix of approaches Windows NT, macOS

docs.title: 1.7 — Monolithic Kernel
docs.text:
The structure 
┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Scheduler  Memory  FS  Network      │
│  Drivers    IPC     Security         │
│         (single address space)        │
└──────────────────────────────────────┘
???+ info "Pros" - **Fast** — direct function calls between subsystems. - **Simple** — one linking model, one debugger. - **Mature** — decades of optimisation. ???+ info "Cons" - **Large** — Linux kernel is ~30 million lines. - **Fragile** — one buggy driver can crash the whole kernel. - **Hard to maintain** — subsystems interlink. !!! tip "Why Linux is monolithic today" Linux started as a monolithic kernel (1991) and remains one. Efforts to add microkernel features (FUSE for user-space filesystems, eBPF for programmable kernel extensions) soften the monolithic edges, but the core design has not changed.

docs.title: 1.8 — Layered Structure
docs.text:
The layered OS (Dijkstra 1968) 
Layer 5 ── User programs
Layer 4 ── I/O management
Layer 3 ── Memory management
Layer 2 ── Process scheduling
Layer 1 ── Memory and I/O primitives
Layer 0 ── Hardware
???+ info "The rule" Layer $N$ may call **only** layer $N-1$. There is no upward or same-layer call. ???+ info "Pros" - **Clean design** — each layer is testable in isolation. - **Well-documented interface** — each layer's API is clear. ???+ warning "Cons" - **Performance** — every operation crosses multiple layers. - **Hard to define layers** — some operations need to skip layers. - **Rarely used in practice** — the THE OS is the classic example.

docs.title: 1.9 — Microkernel
docs.text:
The structure 
┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  User space: FS, drivers, network servers │
├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Kernel: IPC + scheduling + basic memory  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┘
???+ info "The three principles" 1. **Minimal kernel** — only IPC, scheduling, and low-level memory. 2. **All services user-space** — file systems and drivers run as processes. 3. **Message passing** — services communicate via kernel IPC. ???+ info "Pros" - **Reliability** — a crashed driver is a crashed process, restarted by the kernel. - **Security** — the attack surface in kernel mode is tiny. - **Formal verification** — **seL4** is a formally verified microkernel. ???+ info "Cons" - **Performance** — every system call becomes a message round trip. - **Complexity** — IPC must be fast and correct. !!! tip "Where microkernels live" QNX (automotive, medical), MINIX 3 (embedded), seL4 (defence, aerospace), macOS's **Mach** layer (hybrid). The performance gap has narrowed — QNX's IPC is ~1 µs.

docs.title: 1.10 — Computer System Organisation
docs.text:
┌───────────┐        ┌──────────┐        ┌───────────┐
│    CPU    │◄──────►│  Memory  │◄──────►│   DMA     │
└─────┬─────┘  Bus   └──────────┘  Bus   └─────┬─────┘
      │                                       │
      └──────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                 │
           ┌─────▼─────┐
           │   Disk    │
           └───────────┘
???+ note "The four components" - **CPU** — executes instructions, manages registers. - **Memory** — holds instructions and data. - **Buses** — carry addresses, data, and control signals. - **Devices** — disks, network, keyboard, display. !!! tip "The bootstrap sequence" 1. Power on → CPU fetches instruction from address 0. 2. **BIOS/UEFI firmware** runs from ROM. 3. Firmware loads the **bootloader** from disk. 4. Bootloader loads the **kernel** into memory. 5. Kernel initialises devices, memory, scheduler. 6. Kernel launches **init** (or **systemd**), which starts user services.

docs.title: 1.11 — Interrupts
docs.text:
Definition

An interrupt is a signal that causes the CPU to suspend its current execution and transfer control to an interrupt handler.

???+ note "Three types" | Type | Source | Example | |---|---|---| | **Hardware interrupt** | External device | Timer expires, disk completes | | **Trap / exception** | Current instruction | Divide by zero, page fault | | **Software interrupt** | Explicit instruction | System call (`int 0x80` on x86) | ???+ note "The interrupt vector table" Each interrupt is assigned a **number**. The **IVT** maps the number to the handler's address. 
IVT[0]  → divide_error_handler
IVT[14] → page_fault_handler
IVT[32] → timer_handler
IVT[33] → keyboard_handler
???+ info "What happens on interrupt" 1. CPU saves the current **program counter** and **flags** on the stack. 2. CPU switches to **kernel mode** (privileged). 3. CPU jumps to the handler address from the IVT. 4. Handler runs, may signal the waiting process. 5. **`iret`** (interrupt return) restores the previous state. 6. CPU resumes the interrupted program.

docs.title: Worked example 1.1 — Trace a keyboard interrupt
docs.text:
Problem:

A program is running a calculation. The user presses 'A'. Trace the sequence.

???+ note "**Step 1 — hardware.**" Keyboard controller raises IRQ 1 (interrupt request line 1). The CPU, if not masked, accepts the interrupt. ??? info "**Step 2 — save state.**" CPU pushes PC, flags, and register state onto the kernel stack. Switches to ring 0. ??? info "**Step 3 — dispatch.**" CPU jumps to the keyboard handler address from the IVT (typically `IVT[33]` if vector numbers are shifted). ??? info "**Step 4 — handler.**" Reads the scancode from the keyboard controller port. Translates it to 'A'. Places 'A' in the input buffer. Signals any process waiting for keyboard input. ??? info "**Step 5 — return.**" Handler executes `iret`. CPU restores PC and flags. Resumes the calculation. The 'A' is now available for the next `read()` system call. ??? success "**Observation.**" The calculation **never noticed** the interrupt — except for a microsecond of delay. This is the fundamental abstraction of interrupts: **transparent preemption**.

docs.title: 1.12 — Dual-Mode Operation
docs.text: The two modes Mode Privilege What runs Kernel mode (ring 0 on x86) Full hardware access The OS kernel User mode (rings 1–3) Restricted Applications   ???+ info "The mode bit"     The CPU status register contains a **mode bit**:     - `0` = kernel mode (privileged instructions allowed).     - `1` = user mode (privileged instructions trap to the kernel).     ???+ note "Privileged instructions"     Instructions that only the kernel can execute:     - **Halt** the CPU.     - **Disable interrupts**.     - **Load the page table base register**.     - **Direct I/O port access**.     - **Modify the mode bit itself**.     !!! warning "Why this matters"     Without dual-mode operation, a buggy user program could **disable interrupts** and hang the machine, or **reprogram the disk controller** and corrupt the disk. Dual-mode is the foundation of OS protection.

docs.title: 1.13 — System Calls
docs.text:
Definition

A system call is the mechanism by which a user-space program requests a service from the kernel.

???+ note "The three-step sequence" 
User:   write(1, "hello", 5)
          │  (library wrapper)
          ▼
User:   mov $1, %eax        ← syscall number
        syscall             ← trap to kernel
          │
          ▼
Kernel: dispatch to sys_write()
          │  performs the I/O
          ▼
Kernel: iret                ← return to user
          │
          ▼
User:   return from write()
???+ note "Common system calls" | Category | Examples | |---|---| | **Process** | `fork`, `exec`, `exit`, `wait` | | **File** | `open`, `read`, `write`, `close`, `unlink` | | **Memory** | `brk`, `mmap`, `munmap` | | **Network** | `socket`, `bind`, `listen`, `accept`, `connect` | | **Signal** | `kill`, `signal`, `sigaction` | !!! tip "System calls are expensive" A system call involves a mode switch (saving/restoring registers), TLB effects, and cache effects. Typical cost: **500–2000 ns** — compared to a user-space function call at ~1 ns. This is why real programs use **buffered I/O** (e.g., `fwrite` in libc accumulates bytes and issues one `write` per 4 KB).

docs.title: Worked example 1.2 — Trace a write() system call
docs.text:
Problem:

A program calls write(1, "hello\n", 6). Trace the full path.

???+ note "**Step 1 — library wrapper.**" `write()` in libc loads the syscall number for `write` (1 on x86-64) into register `rax`, the file descriptor into `rdi`, the buffer into `rsi`, and the length into `rdx`. ??? info "**Step 2 — trap.**" Executes `syscall` instruction. CPU switches to ring 0, jumps to the kernel's syscall entry point. ??? info "**Step 3 — dispatch.**" Kernel reads `rax`, looks up `sys_call_table[1]` = `sys_write`. Calls it. ??? info "**Step 4 — execute.**" `sys_write` validates the file descriptor (1 = stdout). Copies the 6 bytes to the terminal driver's buffer. Returns 6. ??? info "**Step 5 — return.**" Kernel puts the return value (6) in `rax`. Executes `sysret`. CPU returns to ring 3 at the instruction after `syscall`. ??? success "**Observation.**" The program sees a normal function returning 6. The mode switch, validation, and I/O were all **transparent** — the abstraction worked.

docs.title: 1.14 — Kernel Data Structures
docs.text: What the kernel needs to track Data structure Purpose Process control block (PCB) Per-process state (Chapter 2) Page tables Virtual-to-physical mappings (Chapter 6) Inode table Open file descriptors (Chapter 7) Buffer cache Cached disk blocks (Chapter 8) Run queue Runnable processes (Chapter 3)   !!! tip "The kernel as a giant data structure"     Modern kernels are, in large part, **data-structure management systems**. The scheduler manages the run queue; the memory manager manages the page tables; the file system manages inodes. Understanding the kernel means understanding these structures.

docs.title: 1.15 — Real-World OS Examples
docs.text: The three dominant families Family Examples Architecture Key trait Unix-like Linux, macOS, BSD, Android Monolithic / hybrid Portable, POSIX Windows NT Windows 10/11, Server Hybrid Win32 API, registry Real-time QNX, VxWorks, FreeRTOS Microkernel / small Deterministic   ???+ info "Android's structure"     Android uses a **modified Linux kernel** with a custom **user-space stack**: Bionic libc, ART runtime, Android framework. The kernel is monolithic; the user space is a Java-like managed runtime.     ???+ info "Linux's scale"     - ~30 million lines of code.     - ~2,000 contributors per release.     - Runs on mobile (Android), servers (AWS, GCP), supercomputers (100% of TOP500), embedded (routers, cars).

docs.title: Chapter 1 — key takeaways
docs.text: **1.** An **OS** is an intermediary between user and hardware, providing **convenience** and **efficient resource utilisation**.     **2.** Four resources managed: **CPU, memory, storage, I/O** — each with its own subsystem.     **3.** The OS's evolution — batch → multiprogramming → time-sharing → virtualisation — each step increased **utilisation** and **interactivity**.     **4.** Five kernel structures: **monolithic** (fast but fragile), **layered** (clean but slow), **microkernel** (reliable but IPC-heavy), **modular** (hybrid), **hybrid** (Windows/macOS).     **5.** **Interrupts** enable transparent preemption; the CPU saves state, dispatches to a handler, and returns.     **6.** **Dual-mode operation** (kernel vs user) protects the OS — privileged instructions trap to the kernel.     **7.** **System calls** are the interface — mode switch + dispatch + service + return. Cost: ~1 µs.

docs.title: Next — Chapter 2
docs.text:
Processes.

- The **process concept**: program in execution, memory layout, PCB. - The **five-state model** — new, ready, running, waiting, terminated. - **Process operations**: `fork`, `exec`, `wait`, `exit`. - **Threads**: models, benefits, and the context switch. - **Inter-process communication** basics. Chapter 1 described the OS's role. Chapter 2 describes its first job — **managing processes**.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text: 1. Define a **process** and describe its **memory layout** and **process control block**.     2. Draw and explain the **five-state process model** with every transition.     3. Trace the **fork–exec–wait** sequence for process creation.     4. Distinguish **zombie** and **orphan** processes and explain how to reap them.     5. Compare **thread models**: many-to-one, one-to-one, many-to-many.     6. Measure and analyse **context switch overhead**.

docs.title: 2.1 — What is a Process?
docs.text:
Definition (Tanenbaum §2.1)

A process is a program in execution. It consists of the program code, the current activity (program counter, registers), a stack, a data section, and a heap.

???+ info "Program ≠ process" - A **program** is a passive entity: a binary file on disk. - A **process** is an active entity: a running instance of that program with its own state. One program can have many processes running (e.g., multiple Chrome tabs = multiple processes). !!! tip "The two Chrome models" - **Chrome**: one process per tab. A crashed tab doesn't take down the browser, but memory usage is high. - **Firefox (older versions)**: many tabs in one process. Memory-efficient but one crash loses all tabs. The choice is a classic reliability-vs-resource trade-off.

docs.title: 2.2 — Process Memory Layout
docs.text:
High address
┌─────────────────┐
│     Stack       │  ← local variables, return addresses
│        ↓        │     (grows downward)
│                 │
│                 │
│        ↑        │
│      Heap       │  ← malloc / new (grows upward)
├─────────────────┤
│   Data (BSS)    │  ← uninitialised globals
├─────────────────┤
│   Data (init)   │  ← initialised globals
├─────────────────┤
│     Text        │  ← program code
└─────────────────┘
Low address
???+ note "The five segments" | Segment | Contents | Size | |---|---|---| | **Text** | Machine code | Fixed | | **Data (initialised)** | Global/static with values | Fixed | | **BSS** | Global/static without values | Fixed | | **Heap** | `malloc`/`new` allocations | Dynamic | | **Stack** | Local variables, function frames | Dynamic | !!! warning "Stack and heap grow toward each other" The stack grows **down** (toward lower addresses); the heap grows **up**. They share the same region. When they meet, you have **stack overflow** or **heap overflow**. This is why deep recursion crashes with "stack overflow".

docs.title: 2.3 — The Process Control Block
docs.text:
Definition (Silberschatz §3.1)

The PCB (or task control block) is the data structure the OS uses to track a process. One PCB per process.

???+ note "PCB contents" | Field | Contents | |---|---| | **Process state** | new, ready, running, waiting, terminated | | **Program counter** | Address of the next instruction | | **CPU registers** | Saved on context switch (rax, rbx, ..., rip, rflags) | | **CPU scheduling info** | Priority, time quantum remaining | | **Memory-management info** | Base/limit registers, page-table base | | **Accounting info** | CPU time used, process ID, parent ID | | **I/O status** | Open files, allocated devices | !!! tip "Where does the PCB live?" In the **kernel** (kernel memory, not user memory). It is created at process creation and destroyed at process exit. The kernel's process table is the collection of all PCBs.

docs.title: 2.4 — The Five-State Model
docs.text:
admitted
      new ──────────────► ready ◄───────────────┐
                            │                    │
                            │ scheduler          │ interrupt
                            │ dispatch           │ (preemption)
                            ▼                    │
                          running ───────────────┘
                            │
                            │ I/O or event wait
                            ▼
                         waiting
                            │
                            │ I/O or event completes
                            ▼
                         (back to ready)

                          running ─── exit ───► terminated
???+ note "The five states" | State | Meaning | |---|---| | **New** | Being created | | **Ready** | Waiting for the CPU | | **Running** | Executing on the CPU | | **Waiting** | Waiting for an I/O event | | **Terminated** | Finished; resources being reclaimed |

docs.title: 2.5 — Every Transition, Explained
docs.text: Six transitions Transition Trigger new → ready OS admits the process (enough resources) ready → running Scheduler selects the process running → ready Interrupt (time slice expires) or preemption running → waiting Process requests I/O waiting → ready I/O completes running → terminated Process exits (exit() or crash) !!! warning "The forbidden transition" **waiting → running** is not allowed. A process that finishes I/O must go through **ready** and wait for the scheduler. This preserves fairness — the scheduler decides who runs next. ???+ info "Why five states, not three?" A naive model has only ready, running, waiting. The five-state model adds **new** and **terminated** to represent resource allocation and cleanup phases. This matters in real systems — process creation can be expensive (fork copies memory), and process termination is not instantaneous.

docs.title: Worked example 2.1 — Trace the state of one process
docs.text:
Problem:

A process begins. It runs for 20 ms, then reads from disk (5 ms), then runs for 10 ms, then exits. The scheduler gives it a 15 ms time quantum.

???+ note "**Step 1 — creation.**" Process enters **new**. The kernel allocates the PCB, memory, and initial state. Transitions to **ready**. ??? info "**Step 2 — first scheduling.**" Scheduler picks the process. **ready → running** at t=0. ??? info "**Step 3 — time slice expires.**" At t=15 ms, the timer interrupt fires. **running → ready**. Process is preempted. ??? info "**Step 4 — rescheduled.**" Scheduler picks it again (no other process ready). **ready → running** at t=15. ??? info "**Step 5 — I/O.**" At t=20 ms (5 ms into second slice), process issues a read. **running → waiting**. Disk seek + read takes 5 ms. ??? info "**Step 6 — I/O completes.**" At t=25 ms, disk interrupt. **waiting → ready**. Process is now ready to run. ??? info "**Step 7 — rescheduled.**" Scheduler picks it. **ready → running** at t=25. Runs for 10 ms. ??? info "**Step 8 — exit.**" At t=35 ms, process calls `exit()`. **running → terminated**. ??? success "**Total time.** 35 ms wall clock; 30 ms CPU time; 5 ms blocked on I/O. **CPU utilisation = 30/35 ≈ 86%.**"

docs.title: 2.6 — Process Creation: fork()
Worked example 2.2 — Trace fork() with two processes
docs.text:
Problem:

int main() {
    printf("start\n");
    pid_t pid = fork();
    printf("after fork\n");
    return 0;
}
How many times is each line printed?

???+ note "**Step 1 — before fork.**" One process running. Prints "start". Call `fork()`. ??? info "**Step 2 — fork returns.**" Two processes now exist: - Parent: `pid > 0` (the child's PID). - Child: `pid == 0`. ??? info "**Step 3 — both print.**" Both execute `printf("after fork\n")`. Both exit. ??? success "**Result.**" **"start" printed once** (before fork). **"after fork" printed twice** (once per process). Total output: 
start
after fork
after fork
!!! warning "The order is non-deterministic" The parent and child run **concurrently**. The order of the two "after fork" lines depends on the scheduler. Do not rely on it.

docs.title: Worked example 2.3 — Trace fork() twice
docs.text:
Problem:

fork();
fork();
fork();
printf("hello\n");
How many "hello" lines are printed?

???+ note "**Step 1 — analyse.**" Each `fork()` doubles the number of processes. - Start: 1 process. - After 1st fork: 2 processes. - After 2nd fork: 4 processes. - After 3rd fork: 8 processes. ??? success "**Result.**" **8 lines** of "hello". ???+ info "**Generalisation.**" $n$ consecutive `fork()` calls produce $2^n$ processes. This is the **fork bomb** pattern — and a simple way to exhaust process-table entries.

docs.title: 2.7 — exec() and wait()
docs.text:
exec() — replace the process image

exec() (actually a family: execl, execv, execvp, execle) replaces the calling process's image with a new program. The PID stays the same; the code, data, and stack are replaced.

???+ note "`wait()` — collect the child's exit status" `wait(&status)` blocks the parent until a child terminates. It returns the child's PID and stores its exit status in `status`. ???+ note "The typical pattern" 
pid_t pid = fork();
if (pid == 0) {
    execl("/bin/ls", "ls", "-l", NULL);
    perror("exec");  // only reached if exec fails
    exit(1);
}
wait(NULL);  // wait for the child
!!! tip "Why fork + exec, not just spawn?" The fork-then-exec pattern lets the child **set up the environment** (file descriptors, working directory, signals, resource limits) between `fork()` and `exec()`. This is why Unix shells can implement redirection (`ls > out.txt`) — the child opens `out.txt` and dups it onto fd 1 before `exec`.

docs.title: Worked example 2.4 — A shell command
docs.text:
Problem:

A shell receives ls -l > out.txt. Trace the system calls.

???+ note "**Step 1 — fork.**" Shell calls `fork()`. Child is a copy of the shell. ??? info "**Step 2 — setup (in child).**" Child opens `out.txt` for writing — gets fd 3. Duplicates fd 3 onto fd 1: `dup2(3, 1)`. Now stdout goes to the file. Closes fd 3. ??? info "**Step 3 — exec.**" Child calls `execl("/bin/ls", "ls", "-l", NULL)`. The shell code is replaced by `ls`. ??? info "**Step 4 — parent waits.**" Parent (shell) calls `wait()`. Blocks until `ls` exits. ??? info "**Step 5 — resume.**" `wait()` returns. Shell prints the prompt and waits for the next command. ??? success "**Observation.**" The shell itself never runs `ls` — it creates a child that becomes `ls`. This isolation is why a crashed command does not crash the shell.

docs.title: 2.8 — Zombies and Orphans
docs.text:
Zombie process

A process that has terminated but whose exit status has not been read by the parent. The PCB remains allocated; the process appears in ps as <defunct>.

???+ note "Orphan process" A process whose **parent has terminated** before it. The orphan is re-parented to `init` (PID 1) or `systemd`, which eventually reaps it. ???+ info "How zombies are created" 
pid_t pid = fork();
if (pid == 0) exit(0);       // child exits immediately
sleep(3600);                  // parent sleeps; does NOT call wait()
The child becomes a zombie — its PCB cannot be freed because the parent might call `wait()` later. ???+ success "How zombies are reaped" - **Explicit:** parent calls `wait()` or `waitpid()`. - **Implicit:** parent exits → init/systemd reaps the zombie. !!! warning "The zombie apocalypse" A buggy daemon that forks many children and never waits will accumulate zombies. Eventually the process table fills, and `fork()` fails. This is a real operational risk — monitoring zombie counts is standard practice.

docs.title: 2.9 — Context Switching
docs.text:
Definition

A context switch saves the state of the running process and loads the state of the next process, so that the scheduler can move from one to another.

???+ note "What is saved and restored?" | Component | Cost | |---|---| | **CPU registers** | ~100 ns (save/restore) | | **Program counter** | Included in registers | | **Memory map** | TLB flush or tagged TLB | | **Cache state** | Cold cache after switch | ???+ info "The cost" - **Direct cost:** register save/restore — ~100–500 ns. - **Indirect cost:** cache and TLB effects — often **10× the direct cost**. !!! tip "Why context switch is expensive" When you switch processes, the new process's working set is not in cache. The first thousands of memory accesses miss. This is why **thread context switches** (same address space, no TLB flush) are much cheaper than **process context switches**.

docs.title: Worked example 2.5 — Context switch overhead
docs.text:
Problem:

A context switch costs 5 µs. A system does 1000 switches per second. What fraction of CPU time is spent switching?

???+ note "**Step 1 — total switch time per second.**" $1000 \times 5\ \mu\text{s} = 5000\ \mu\text{s} = 5\ \text{ms}$. ??? info "**Step 2 — fraction of one second.**" $5\ \text{ms} / 1000\ \text{ms} = 0.5\%$. ??? success "**Result.**" **0.5%** of CPU time. This seems small — but if the time quantum is 10 ms and a switch is 5 µs, the effective utilisation is $10/(10 + 0.005) \approx 99.95\%$. ???+ warning "**The catch.**" The **indirect** cost (cache and TLB) is often **5–10×** the direct cost. Real overhead is closer to **5%** in context-switch-heavy workloads.

docs.title: 2.10 — Threads
docs.text:
Definition

A thread is the smallest unit of execution within a process. Each thread has its own program counter, register set, and stack, but shares code, data, and open files with other threads in the same process.

???+ note "What threads share vs. have" | Shared | Per-thread | |---|---| | Code segment | Program counter | | Data segment | Registers | | Heap | Stack | | Open files | Thread-local storage (optional) | | Signal handlers | Signal mask | ???+ info "Creating threads" - **POSIX pthreads:** `pthread_create(&tid, NULL, func, arg)`. - **Java:** `new Thread(runnable).start()`. - **Python:** `threading.Thread(target=func).start()` (but GIL limits true parallelism).

docs.title: 2.11 — Benefits of Threads
docs.text: Four benefits (Silberschatz §4.2) Benefit Description Responsiveness UI thread stays responsive while worker threads compute Resource sharing Threads share memory — no IPC needed Economy Thread creation/switch is cheaper than process Scalability Threads run in parallel on multicore CPUs   ???+ info "The economy comparison"     | Operation | Process | Thread |     |---|---|---|     | Create | ~10–30 µs | ~1–2 µs |     | Context switch | ~5–10 µs | ~0.5–1 µs |     | Memory overhead | Full address space | Stack + minimal |     !!! tip "The responsiveness argument"     A web server can spawn one thread per client. While one thread blocks on a slow client, others serve requests. Without threads, the server would handle clients one at a time (or need `select()`-based multiplexing).

docs.title: 2.12 — Thread Models
docs.text:
User threads vs kernel threads
  • User threads — managed by a library (e.g., green threads). The kernel does not know they exist.
  • Kernel threads — managed by the kernel. Scheduled independently.
???+ note "The three mappings" | Model | Description | Example | |---|---|---| | **Many-to-one** | Many user threads → one kernel thread | Old Java (green threads), some embedded | | **One-to-one** | Each user thread → one kernel thread | Linux, Windows, macOS | | **Many-to-many** | Many user threads → smaller number of kernel threads | Solaris (older), Go goroutines (partially) | ???+ info "Trade-offs" | Model | Pros | Cons | |---|---|---| | Many-to-one | Fast; no kernel context switches | One blocking thread blocks all; no parallelism | | One-to-one | True parallelism; blocking is per-thread | More overhead; kernel thread limit | | Many-to-many | Best of both | Complex to implement | !!! tip "What modern OSes actually use" Linux and Windows use **one-to-one** — each user thread is a kernel thread. Modern hardware has eliminated most of the overhead that many-to-one was designed to avoid. Many-to-many exists mostly in language runtimes (Go's goroutines, Erlang's processes).

docs.title: Worked example 2.6 — Threads vs processes
docs.text:
Problem:

A program computes 100 tasks, each CPU-bound for 10 ms, on a 4-core CPU. Compare using 4 processes vs 4 threads.

???+ note "**Step 1 — 4 processes.**" - Creation cost: $4 \times 25\ \mu\text{s} = 100\ \mu\text{s}$. - Context switch cost: $4 \times 10\ \mu\text{s} = 40\ \mu\text{s}$ per round. - Memory: 4 separate address spaces (4× memory). ??? info "**Step 2 — 4 threads.**" - Creation cost: $4 \times 1.5\ \mu\text{s} = 6\ \mu\text{s}$. - Context switch cost: $4 \times 1\ \mu\text{s} = 4\ \mu\text{s}$ per round. - Memory: one address space, 4 stacks. ??? info "**Step 3 — compute time.**" Each core processes 25 tasks in parallel: $25 \times 10\ \text{ms} = 250\ \text{ms}$. Total time (threads) ≈ $250\ \text{ms} + 6\ \mu\text{s} + 4\ \mu\text{s} \approx 250\ \text{ms}$. Total time (processes) ≈ $250\ \text{ms} + 100\ \mu\text{s} + 40\ \mu\text{s} \approx 250\ \text{ms}$. ??? success "**Conclusion.**" For **CPU-bound work with no sharing**, threads and processes are similar in total time — but threads use **much less memory** and have lower overhead. For **I/O-bound work**, threads win **decisively** because a blocked I/O doesn't block the whole process.

docs.title: 2.13 — Inter-Process Communication (IPC) Preview
docs.text:
Why IPC?

Processes are isolated by design — one process cannot directly access another's memory. To cooperate, they need an OS-mediated channel.

???+ note "Three IPC mechanisms" | Mechanism | Direction | Data | |---|---|---| | **Pipes** | Unidirectional | Byte stream | | **Message queues** | Bidirectional | Structured messages | | **Shared memory** | Bidirectional | Raw memory (fastest) | !!! tip "Shared memory is the fastest" After the initial setup, shared memory requires no kernel involvement — processes read and write directly. But it also requires **synchronization** (Chapter 4) — the OS cannot prevent race conditions on shared memory.

docs.title: Chapter 2 — key takeaways
docs.text: **1.** A **process** is a running program with memory (text, data, bss, heap, stack) and a **PCB** tracking its state.     **2.** The **five-state model** (new, ready, running, waiting, terminated) captures process lifecycle; **waiting → running** is forbidden.     **3.** `fork()` creates a child; `exec()` replaces the image; `wait()` collects the exit status. This three-call pattern is the Unix process model.     **4.** **Zombies** (terminated but unreaped) and **orphans** (re-parented) are process states to monitor; zombies fill the process table.     **5.** **Context switch** saves/restores state — direct cost ~µs, indirect cost (cache/TLB) 5–10× that.     **6.** **Threads** share address space; per-thread state is small. Benefits: responsiveness, sharing, economy, scalability.     **7.** **Thread models:** many-to-one (fast, no parallelism), one-to-one (Linux/Windows), many-to-many (Go, Erlang). Modern OSes use one-to-one.

docs.title: Next — Chapter 3
docs.text:
CPU Scheduling.

- **Scheduling criteria:** CPU utilisation, throughput, turnaround, waiting, response. - **Algorithms:** FCFS, SJF, SRTN, Round Robin, priority, MLFQ. - **Traces** — waiting-time computations on real workloads. - **Multiprocessor** scheduling, affinity. - **Real-time** scheduling — RM and EDF. Chapter 2 described the process. Chapter 3 describes how the OS **decides which process to run next** — the scheduler.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text: 1. Distinguish **preemptive** from **non-preemptive** scheduling.     2. Compute the five **scheduling criteria** for a given workload.     3. Trace **FCFS**, **SJF**, **SRTN**, **Round Robin**, **priority**, and **MLFQ** on a workload.     4. Analyse **priority inversion** and its fix.     5. Compare **RM** and **EDF** for real-time scheduling.

docs.title: 3.1 — Why CPU Scheduling?
docs.text:
The core problem

A single-core CPU can run one process at a time. Many processes are ready to run. The scheduler decides which one.

???+ info "The scheduling loop" 
while (true):
    if (no ready process):
        idle
    else:
        pick = choose(ready_queue)
        dispatch(pick)
        wait for interrupt (I/O, timer, syscall)
!!! tip "Multiprogramming keeps the CPU busy" Without scheduling, the CPU would idle whenever the running process blocked on I/O. The scheduler switches to another process — this is what makes multiprogramming valuable.

docs.title: 3.2 — Preemptive vs Non-Preemptive
docs.text:
When is scheduling triggered?

The scheduler can run on any of four events:

  1. Running → waiting (I/O request).
  2. Running → ready (interrupt / preemption).
  3. Waiting → ready (I/O completes).
  4. Running → terminated (exit).
???+ note "Two modes" | Mode | Scheduling happens on | |---|---| | **Non-preemptive** | Events 1 and 4 only (running process must yield) | | **Preemptive** | All four events (OS can interrupt) | ???+ info "Examples" - **Non-preemptive** — old Windows 3.1, basic batch systems. - **Preemptive** — modern Linux, Windows, macOS. **All interactive OSes are preemptive.** !!! warning "Preemption has costs" Every preemption = one context switch = cache pollution + TLB flush. Preemptive schedulers pay overhead for responsiveness.

docs.title: 3.3 — The Five Scheduling Criteria
docs.text: Definitions (Silberschatz §5.2) Criterion Definition Goal CPU utilisation % time CPU is doing useful work maximise Throughput Processes completed per time unit maximise Turnaround time Completion time − arrival time minimise Waiting time Time spent in ready queue minimise Response time Time from submission to first response minimise   ???+ info "Turnaround vs waiting"     - **Turnaround** includes I/O wait and CPU time.     - **Waiting** counts only ready-queue time.      $T_{\text{turnaround}} = T_{\text{waiting}} + T_{\text{CPU}} + T_{\text{I/O}}$.     !!! warning "No algorithm optimises all five"     FCFS gives good throughput but poor response. RR gives good response but frequent switches. The choice depends on whether the workload is **batch, interactive, or real-time**.

docs.title: 3.4 — First-Come, First-Served (FCFS)
docs.text:
The algorithm

Processes are served in arrival order. Non-preemptive.

Ready queue:  [P1] → [P2] → [P3] → [P4]
CPU:          runs P1 to completion, then P2, ...
???+ info "Pros and cons" - **Pros:** Simple, no starvation, low overhead. - **Cons:** **Convoy effect** — a long process at the head of the queue makes all shorter processes wait. ???+ note "The convoy effect" | Process | Burst | |---|---| | P1 | 100 | | P2 | 1 | | P3 | 1 | | P4 | 1 | FCFS order: P1, P2, P3, P4. Wait times: P1=0, P2=100, P3=101, P4=102. **Average wait = 75.75.** SJF would give 0.75.

docs.title: 3.5 — Shortest Job First (SJF)
docs.text:
The algorithm

Choose the process with the smallest burst time. Non-preemptive.

???+ abstract "Theorem (Silberschatz §5.3)" **SJF is optimal** for average waiting time among non-preemptive algorithms. ???+ info "Proof sketch (exchange argument)" Suppose an optimal schedule has two adjacent jobs A, B with $A.\text{burst} > B.\text{burst}$ and A before B. Swap them: - Waiting time of A increases by $B.\text{burst}$. - Waiting time of B decreases by $A.\text{burst}$. - Net change: $B - A < 0$ — the average waiting time **decreases**. So any schedule with a longer job before a shorter one can be improved → SJF is optimal. !!! warning "The practical problem" SJF requires **knowing burst times in advance** — impossible in general. Solutions: - **User estimation** (type the burst time when submitting). - **Exponential averaging** — predict the next burst from past bursts. ???+ info "Exponential averaging" $\tau_{n+1} = \alpha \cdot t_n + (1-\alpha) \cdot \tau_n$ where $t_n$ is the actual burst, $\tau_n$ the previous prediction, and $\alpha \in [0,1]$ (typically $\alpha = 0.5$). This predicts the next burst from a weighted average of the past.

docs.title: 3.6 — Shortest Remaining Time Next (SRTN)
docs.text:
The algorithm

Preemptive version of SJF. When a new process arrives with a shorter remaining time than the running process, preempt.

???+ info "SJF vs SRTN" - **SJF:** choose shortest burst, run to completion. - **SRTN:** choose shortest **remaining**, preempt if a shorter job arrives. ???+ success "SRTN is optimal for average waiting time" Among **all** preemptive or non-preemptive algorithms, SRTN minimises average waiting time. !!! warning "SRTN can starve long jobs" If short jobs keep arriving, a long job may never run. This is **starvation** — the price of optimal average wait.

docs.title: Worked example 3.1 — FCFS vs SJF vs SRTN
docs.text:
Problem:

Process Arrival Burst P1 0 8 P2 1 4 P3 2 9 P4 3 5 ???+ note "**FCFS** — order by arrival." | P | Wait | |---|---| | P1 | 0 | | P2 | 7 | | P3 | 10 | | P4 | 17 | | **Avg** | **8.5** | ??? info "**SJF (non-preemptive)** — order by burst." Order: P2 (4), P4 (5), P1 (8), P3 (9). | P | Arrival | Start | Wait | |---|---|---|---| | P2 | 1 | 1 | 0 | | P4 | 3 | 5 | 2 | | P1 | 0 | 10 | 10 | | P3 | 2 | 18 | 16 | | **Avg** | | | **7.0** | ??? info "**SRTN** — preempt when shorter arrives." - t=0: P1 starts (remaining 8). - t=1: P2 arrives (4 < 7). Preempt P1, run P2. - t=5: P2 done. P4 (5) vs P1 (7) vs P3 (9). Run P4. - t=10: P4 done. P1 (7) vs P3 (9). Run P1. - t=17: P1 done. Run P3. | P | Arrival | Start | Wait | |---|---|---|---| | P2 | 1 | 1 | 0 | | P4 | 3 | 5 | 2 | | P1 | 0 | 10 | 10 | | P3 | 2 | 17 | 15 | | **Avg** | | | **6.75** | ??? success "**Observation.**" SRTN (6.75) < SJF (7.0) < FCFS (8.5). Preemption buys a small improvement but risks starvation.

docs.title: 3.7 — Round Robin (RR)
docs.text:
The algorithm

Each process gets a time quantum \(q\). When the quantum expires, the process is preempted and placed at the tail of the ready queue.

Ready queue: [P1] → [P2] → [P3] → [P4]
CPU: runs P1 for q, then P2 for q, ...  (circular)
???+ info "Behaviour depends on $q$" | $q$ | Behaviour | |---|---| | **Very small** ($q <$ context switch) | Context switch overhead dominates | | **Too large** ($q >$ burst times) | Degenerates to FCFS | | **Just right** | Fair, responsive, low overhead | ???+ tip "Rule of thumb" $q$ should be **large enough** that 80% of CPU bursts are shorter than $q$. Typical values: **10–100 ms** for interactive systems. ???+ info "Pros and cons" - **Pros:** Fair (no starvation), responsive (short jobs finish quickly), simple. - **Cons:** Higher average waiting time than SJF; context switch overhead.

docs.title: Worked example 3.2 — Round Robin trace
docs.text:
Problem:

Same workload as 3.1: P1(0, 8), P2(1, 4), P3(2, 9), P4(3, 5). \(q = 4\).

???+ note "**Timeline.**" | Time | Running | Ready queue | |---|---|---| | 0–4 | P1 | P2, P3, P4, P1 | | 4–8 | P2 | P3, P4, P1 | | 8–12 | P3 | P4, P1, P3 | | 12–16 | P4 | P1, P3, P4 | | 16–20 | P1 | P3, P4 | | 20–24 | P3 | P4, P3 | | 24–26 | P4 | P3 | | 26–29 | P3 | — | ??? info "**Compute waiting times.**" - P1: finishes at 20. Burst 8. Waiting = $20 - 0 - 8 = 12$. - P2: finishes at 8. Burst 4. Waiting = $8 - 1 - 4 = 3$. - P3: finishes at 29. Burst 9. Waiting = $29 - 2 - 9 = 18$. - P4: finishes at 26. Burst 5. Waiting = $26 - 3 - 5 = 18$. **Average wait = (12 + 3 + 18 + 18) / 4 = 12.75.** ??? success "**Observation.**" RR's average wait (12.75) is **worse** than SJF (7.0) — but RR gives every process a fair share. This is the price of **responsiveness**.

docs.title: 3.8 — Priority Scheduling
docs.text:
The algorithm

Each process has a priority. The highest-priority ready process runs. Can be preemptive or non-preemptive.

???+ info "Priority assignment" - **Static** — assigned once at creation (e.g., "system process has priority 0, user priority 50"). - **Dynamic** — changes with behaviour (e.g., I/O-bound gets higher priority). ???+ warning "Priority inversion" A **high-priority** task waits for a resource held by a **low-priority** task, while a **medium-priority** task preempts the low-priority holder. The high-priority task effectively waits for the medium-priority task.

docs.title: Worked example 3.3 — Priority inversion in detail
docs.text:
Problem:

Three tasks: - H (high priority) needs a lock L. - M (medium priority) is CPU-bound, no locks. - L (low priority) holds L.

Trace the scenario.

???+ note "**Step 1 — L acquires L.**" L starts, acquires L, and begins work. ??? info "**Step 2 — H preempts.**" H arrives, preempts L. H tries to acquire L — blocks because L holds it. L is ready to resume. ??? info "**Step 3 — M arrives.**" M preempts L (M > L in priority). L cannot run. L cannot release L. H waits. ??? info "**Step 4 — the inversion.**" H, the highest priority, is effectively waiting for M, the medium priority — through the low-priority L. This violates the priority ordering. ??? success "**The fix — priority inheritance.**" When H blocks on L, temporarily raise **L's priority to H's level**. Now M cannot preempt L. L runs, releases L, drops back to low priority. H proceeds. !!! tip "The Mars Pathfinder (1997)" The Pathfinder lander experienced repeated reboots due to priority inversion in VxWorks. The fix was a one-line change: enable priority inheritance. Famous case study in real-time systems.

docs.title: 3.9 — Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ)
docs.text:
The algorithm

Multiple ready queues with different priorities and time quanta. Processes move between queues based on behaviour.

Q0 (quantum 8, highest)   ← new processes start here
Q1 (quantum 16)
Q2 (quantum 32, lowest)   ← CPU-bound processes end up here
???+ note "The three rules" 1. If priority(A) > priority(B), run A. 2. If priority(A) = priority(B), round robin. 3. **New processes start at the top** (highest priority). 4. **If a process uses its full quantum, drop one level.** 5. **Periodically boost all processes** to the top (aging). ???+ info "What MLFQ optimises for" - **Interactive processes** (short bursts) stay at the top → fast response. - **CPU-bound processes** sink to the bottom → large quanta, low overhead. - **Periodic boost** prevents starvation. !!! tip "Modern examples" Windows uses a variant of MLFQ with **priority boosts** for I/O-completing processes (a process that just finished I/O gets a temporary priority boost — it's likely interactive).

docs.title: 3.10 — Multiprocessor Scheduling
docs.text: The two approaches Approach Description Asymmetric One master CPU schedules; the others execute Symmetric (SMP) Each CPU schedules itself; shared ready queue   ???+ info "SMP load balancing"     - **Push migration** — a CPU periodically pushes tasks to underloaded CPUs.     - **Pull migration** — an idle CPU steals tasks from overloaded CPUs.     ???+ note "Processor affinity"     - **Soft affinity** — the scheduler tries to keep a process on the same CPU.     - **Hard affinity** — the process is bound to a specific CPU (e.g., `taskset` in Linux).     !!! tip "Why affinity matters"     When a process migrates between CPUs, its working set stays in the old CPU's cache. Re-populating the new CPU's cache costs thousands of cycles. Affinity keeps the cache warm.

docs.title: 3.11 — Real-Time Scheduling
docs.text:
Definition

A real-time system must meet deadlines — a result that arrives late is as bad as no result.

???+ note "Two categories" | Category | Consequence of missing deadline | |---|---| | **Hard real-time** | Catastrophic (airbag, pacemaker) | | **Soft real-time** | Degraded quality (video streaming, VoIP) | ???+ note "Two algorithms" | Algorithm | Priority | Optimal? | |---|---|---| | **Rate Monotonic (RM)** | Static — shorter period = higher priority | Optimal among static-priority | | **Earliest Deadline First (EDF)** | Dynamic — earliest deadline first | Optimal among all preemptive | ???+ info "Schedulability tests" For $n$ periodic tasks with utilisation $U = \sum C_i / T_i$: - **RM** is schedulable if $U \le n(2^{1/n} - 1)$. As $n \to \infty$, this approaches $\ln 2 \approx 0.693$. - **EDF** is schedulable iff $U \le 1$.

docs.title: Worked example 3.4 — RM vs EDF
docs.text:
Problem:

Three periodic tasks: - Task A: \(C=2, T=5\). - Task B: \(C=2, T=7\). - Task C: \(C=3, T=10\).

???+ note "**Step 1 — utilisation.**" $U = 2/5 + 2/7 + 3/10 = 0.4 + 0.286 + 0.3 = 0.986$. ??? info "**Step 2 — RM schedulable?**" $n(2^{1/n} - 1) = 3(2^{1/3} - 1) \approx 3(1.2599 - 1) = 0.78$. $U = 0.986 > 0.78$ → **RM not guaranteed** (may or may not be schedulable — the test is sufficient, not necessary). ??? info "**Step 3 — EDF schedulable?**" $U = 0.986 \le 1$ → **EDF is schedulable**. ✓ ??? success "**Conclusion.**" EDF succeeds where RM fails. This is expected — EDF is optimal, RM is not. But EDF is harder to implement (dynamic priorities), and under overload, EDF's behaviour is "domino effect" — once a deadline is missed, subsequent ones often miss. !!! tip "RM's advantage under overload" Under overload, RM **fails gracefully** — high-priority tasks keep meeting deadlines; low-priority ones miss. EDF **fails catastrophically** — everything misses. This is why RM (with a lower utilisation bound) is preferred in safety-critical systems.

docs.title: 3.12 — Linux's CFS: A Modern Case Study
docs.text:
Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS)

Linux's default scheduler (since 2.6.23). Key idea: track virtual runtime — the amount of CPU time each process has received, weighted by priority.

???+ note "The algorithm" - Each process has a **vruntime** (virtual runtime). - The scheduler always runs the process with the **smallest vruntime**. - Uses a **red-black tree** to find the minimum in $O(\log n)$. - When a process is preempted, its vruntime is updated. ???+ info "Why it's "fair"" Over time, all processes get approximately equal vruntime — meaning equal CPU share. Priority is implemented as a **weight**: a nice -20 process's vruntime advances 1/20th as fast as a nice 0 process, so it gets 20× more CPU. !!! tip "CFS replaced the O(1) scheduler" The previous O(1) scheduler used a fixed-priority multilevel queue. It scaled well but had poor interactive responsiveness. CFS's virtual-runtime model gives smooth fairness without explicit priority boosting.

docs.title: Chapter 3 — key takeaways
docs.text: **1.** **Preemptive** schedulers can interrupt the running process; **non-preemptive** cannot. All interactive OSes are preemptive.     **2.** Five criteria: **utilisation**, **throughput**, **turnaround**, **waiting**, **response** — no algorithm optimises all.     **3.** **FCFS** suffers from convoy effect. **SJF** is optimal for average wait but requires burst-time knowledge. **SRTN** is optimal preemptively but can starve.     **4.** **Round Robin** gives fairness and response time; the quantum trades overhead against responsiveness.     **5.** **MLFQ** adapts to behaviour — interactive processes stay high, CPU-bound sink. Periodic boost prevents starvation.     **6.** **Priority inversion** (H waits for L via M) is fixed by **priority inheritance**.     **7.** **RM** is optimal among static-priority; **EDF** is optimal overall. RM fails gracefully; EDF catastrophically.

docs.text:
Inter-Process Communication and Synchronization.

- **Race conditions** — the fundamental problem. - **Critical section** — the three requirements. - **Peterson's solution** — software mutex for two processes. - **Hardware primitives** — test-and-set, compare-and-swap. - **Semaphores** and **monitors**. - **Classical problems** — producer-consumer, readers-writers, dining philosophers. Chapter 3 scheduled processes on the CPU. Chapter 4 coordinates them — because when processes share data, **chaos** is the default.

Explain **Peterson's solution** and hardware primitives.     4. Use **semaphores** and **monitors** to solve the producer–consumer problem.     5. Solve the **readers–writers** and **dining philosophers** problems without deadlock.

docs.title: 4.1 — Why Synchronization?
docs.text:
The fundamental problem

Processes (and threads) share memory. When two of them read and write the same location concurrently, the final value can depend on the exact order of their instructions.

???+ note "Definition — Race condition" A **race condition** occurs when the outcome of a computation depends on the **relative timing** of two or more concurrent operations on shared data. !!! warning "Race conditions are common" Any shared **counter**, **list**, **queue**, or **cache** is a candidate. Most real-world data corruption bugs — in databases, OS kernels, and networked applications — are race conditions.

docs.title: 4.2 — The Counter Example
4.3 — The Critical Section Problem
4.4 — Peterson's Solution
4.5 — Hardware Primitives
docs.text:
The problem with software-only solutions

They rely on the CPU's memory model. Atomic hardware instructions eliminate that assumption.

???+ note "Test-and-set" 
bool test_and_set(bool* target):
    bool rv = *target
    *target = true
    return rv
**Atomically:** reads the old value and sets to true, in a single instruction. ???+ note "Compare-and-swap (CAS)" 
bool compare_and_swap(int* ptr, int expected, int new):
    if *ptr == expected:
        *ptr = new
        return true
    return false
???+ note "Load-linked / store-conditional (LL/SC)" - **LL** — loads a value and marks the memory address. - **SC** — stores a value only if the address has not changed since LL. More expressive than CAS — allows lock-free algorithms on arbitrary words.

docs.title: 4.6 — Semaphores
docs.text:
Definition (Dijkstra 1965)

A semaphore \(S\) is an integer variable accessed only through two atomic operations:

???+ note "The two operations" 
wait(S):      // also called P() or down()
    S = S - 1
    if S < 0: block

signal(S):    // also called V() or up()
    S = S + 1
    if S <= 0: wake up one blocked process
???+ note "Two types" | Type | Values | Use | |---|---|---| | **Binary semaphore** | 0 or 1 | Acts as a mutex | | **Counting semaphore** | Any non-negative | Controls access to $N$ identical resources | !!! warning "Atomicity" `wait()` and `signal()` are **atomic** — the kernel (or hardware) guarantees no interleaving. Without atomicity, the semaphore itself has a race condition.

docs.title: Worked example 4.1 — Mutex via binary semaphore
docs.text:
Problem:

Two threads increment a shared counter 1,000,000 times each. Use a semaphore to make it correct.

???+ note "**Step 1 — the setup.**" 
sem_t mutex;
sem_init(&mutex, 0, 1);       // initial value 1
int counter = 0;
??? info "**Step 2 — the critical section.**" 
void* worker(void* arg) {
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        sem_wait(&mutex);
        counter++;
        sem_post(&mutex);
    }
    return NULL;
}
??? info "**Step 3 — trace.**" - Thread A calls `sem_wait`: S = 1 → S = 0, proceeds. - Thread B calls `sem_wait`: S = 0 → S = -1, blocks. - Thread A increments counter, calls `sem_post`: S = -1 → S = 0, wakes B. - Thread B proceeds. **Only one thread in the critical section at a time.** ✓ ??? success "**Result.** Final counter = 2,000,000."

docs.title: 4.7 — The Producer-Consumer Problem
Worked example 4.2 — Trace producer-consumer
docs.text:
Problem:

\(N = 3\). Trace the state when a producer inserts 4 items and a consumer removes 2.

???+ note "**Initial:** `empty = 3`, `full = 0`, `mutex = 1`." ??? info "**Producer inserts A.**" `wait(empty)` → empty = 2. `wait(mutex)` → mutex = 0. Insert A. `signal(mutex)` → mutex = 1. `signal(full)` → full = 1. ??? info "**Producer inserts B, C.**" Same pattern. Now: empty = 0, full = 3, mutex = 1. ??? info "**Producer tries D.**" `wait(empty)` → empty = -1, **blocks**. Producer is stuck until a consumer frees a slot. ??? info "**Consumer removes A.**" `wait(full)` → full = 2. `wait(mutex)` → mutex = 0. Remove A. `signal(mutex)` → mutex = 1. `signal(empty)` → empty = 0, **wakes producer**. ??? info "**Producer resumes.**" Producer unblocks from `wait(empty)`, proceeds with `wait(mutex)`, inserts D. `signal(full)` → full = 3. Done. ??? success "**Final state.** empty = 0, full = 3, mutex = 1. Buffer contains B, C, D."

docs.title: 4.8 — Monitors
Worked example 4.3 — Producer-consumer with monitors
docs.text:
Problem:

Same problem, using a monitor.

???+ note "**The monitor.**" 
monitor BoundedBuffer {
    int[] buffer = new int[N];
    int count = 0, in = 0, out = 0;
    condition notFull, notEmpty;

    procedure insert(item) {
        while (count == N) notFull.wait();
        buffer[in] = item;
        in = (in + 1) % N;
        count++;
        notEmpty.signal();
    }

    procedure remove() {
        while (count == 0) notEmpty.wait();
        int item = buffer[out];
        out = (out + 1) % N;
        count--;
        notFull.signal();
        return item;
    }
}
??? info "**Producer:** `BoundedBuffer.insert(item)`." ??? info "**Consumer:** `BoundedBuffer.remove()`." ??? success "**Why this is simpler.**" No explicit `mutex` — the monitor guarantees it. No risk of wrong `wait`/`signal` order — the compiler or runtime handles it.

4.11 — Deadlock vs Starvation
docs.text: Two failure modes Failure Definition Fix Deadlock Two or more processes wait for each other forever Break one Coffman condition (Chapter 5) Starvation A process waits indefinitely because others keep preempting Aging (increase priority of waiters)   !!! tip "Deadlock implies starvation, but not vice versa"     All deadlocked processes are starved — but starved processes are not deadlocked. The distinction matters: deadlock is a **global** condition; starvation is a **local** one.

docs.title: Chapter 4 — key takeaways
docs.text: **1.** **Race conditions** arise when concurrent access to shared data produces non-deterministic results. The counter example makes this concrete.     **2.** The **critical-section problem** has three requirements: **mutual exclusion**, **progress**, **bounded waiting**.     **3.** **Peterson's solution** is a two-process software mutex — elegant but relies on sequential consistency.     **4.** **Hardware primitives** (test-and-set, CAS, LL/SC) provide atomicity at the instruction level.     **5.** **Semaphores** are counting or binary; `wait`/`signal` must be called in the right order to avoid deadlock.     **6.** **Monitors** bundle shared data with procedures and a mutex — easier to use than raw semaphores.     **7.** **Producer-consumer**, **readers-writers**, **dining philosophers** are the canonical synchronization problems — each with known correct solutions.
