docs.title: 5.1 — What is a Deadlock?
docs.text:
Definition (Silberschatz §7.1)

A deadlock is a set of blocked processes, each holding a resource and waiting to acquire a resource held by another process in the set.

???+ note "The simplest example" Two processes, two resources: | Time | P1 | P2 | |---|---|---| | 1 | acquires R1 | | | 2 | | acquires R2 | | 3 | waits for R2 | | | 4 | | waits for R1 | Both processes wait forever. **Deadlock.** !!! warning "Deadlock requires real resources" Resources must be **unshareable** (mutex-held). Shareable resources (read-only files, CPU time slices) cannot cause deadlock. The problem is exclusive access to finite resources.

docs.title: 5.2 — System Resource Model
docs.text:
Resource types and instances

A system has \(m\) resource types, each with \(W_i\) instances.

  • Resource type: printer, disk, mutex, semaphore.
  • Instance: each individual printer, each individual disk block.
???+ note "Process's use of resources" A process uses a resource in three phases: 1. **Request** — ask for the resource; wait if not available. 2. **Use** — hold the resource; do work. 3. **Release** — give the resource back. ???+ info "Formal model" - $n$ processes. - $m$ resource types, with $W_i$ instances of type $i$. - **Allocation matrix** $A$ — $A_{ij}$ = number of type-$j$ resources held by process $i$. - **Request matrix** $R$ — $R_{ij}$ = number of type-$j$ resources process $i$ is requesting. - **Availability vector** $V$ — $V_j$ = free resources of type $j$.

docs.title: 5.3 — The Four Coffman Conditions
docs.text:
Coffman conditions (1971)

A deadlock can occur only if all four of the following hold simultaneously:

???+ note "1. Mutual exclusion" At least one resource is held in a **non-shareable** mode — only one process can use it at a time. ???+ note "2. Hold and wait" A process holding at least one resource is **waiting for additional resources** held by other processes. ???+ note "3. No preemption" Resources **cannot be forcibly taken** from a process. They must be released voluntarily. ???+ note "4. Circular wait" A **circular chain** of processes exists where each waits for a resource held by the next in the chain. ???+ success "The implication" **Breaking any one** of these conditions prevents deadlock. **All four are necessary** — the absence of even one makes deadlock impossible.

docs.title: 5.4 — Resource Allocation Graph
docs.text:
Definition

A resource allocation graph (RAG) is a directed graph where: - Circles are processes. - Rectangles are resource types (with dots for instances). - Edges: - Request — \(P \to R\) (dashed, if using explicit request edges). - Assignment — \(R \to P\).

???+ note "Example RAG" 
P1 ──► R1 ──► P2 ──► R2 ──► P1
P1 holds R2 (implicitly) and requests R1. P2 holds R1 and requests R2. **Cycle → deadlock** (if one instance per resource). ???+ abstract "The RAG rule (single instance)" In a RAG with **one instance per resource**: **A cycle is necessary and sufficient for deadlock.** ???+ warning "The rule breaks for multiple instances" With multiple instances per resource, a cycle is **necessary but not sufficient** — the resources in the cycle might be available elsewhere. This is why we need the detection algorithm (Section 5.8).

docs.title: Worked example 5.1 — Detect deadlock from a RAG
docs.text:
Problem:

P1 ──► R1 ──► P2
              │
              ▼
              R2 ──► P1
Plus: R2 has 2 instances, one held by P1 and one free.

???+ note "**Step 1 — check for cycles.**" P1 → R1 → P2 → R2 → P1. **Cycle exists.** ??? info "**Step 2 — check instances.**" R2 has 2 instances; 1 held by P1, 1 free. P2 requests R2 (1 instance). R2 has a free instance — so P2 can be satisfied. The cycle is **broken** when P2 gets R2's free instance and finishes. ??? success "**Conclusion.**" **No deadlock.** The cycle exists but is **not a deadlock** — a free instance breaks it. This illustrates why the RAG rule requires single instances.

docs.title: 5.5 — Deadlock Prevention
docs.text: Prevent by breaking one condition Condition How to break Cost Mutual exclusion Make resources shareable Often impossible Hold and wait Request all resources at once, or release all before requesting new Low utilisation No preemption Allow preemption Requires save/restore state Circular wait Impose a total order on resources Restricts programming   ???+ note "Hold-and-wait prevention"     Two variants:     1. **Request all at once** — the process requests every resource it will ever need before starting. **Low utilisation** — a process holding resources waits for others.     2. **Release all before requesting new** — the process releases everything before requesting more. **Restart required** — cannot easily resume.     ???+ note "No-preemption prevention"     - When a process requests a resource held by another, **preempt** the holder.     - The preempted process is **rolled back** to a safe state.     - Works only if the state is checkpointable (e.g., CPU registers, but not a partially written file).     ???+ note "Circular-wait prevention (the practical choice)"     Assign a **global order** to all resources (e.g., by resource number). Each process must request resources in **increasing order**. This prevents a cycle — if P1 holds R1 (lower) and requests R2 (higher), and P2 holds R2 and requests R1, P2's request violates the ordering.     !!! tip "The UNIX lock order"     Linux's kernel uses a **lock order** documented in the source tree — every mutex has a level, and acquiring locks out of order triggers a warning (`might_sleep` / lockdep). This is circular-wait prevention in action.

docs.title: 5.6 — Deadlock Avoidance
docs.text:
The idea

Prevention is static and conservative. Avoidance is dynamic: it grants a request only if the resulting state is safe.

???+ abstract "Safe state (Silberschatz §7.5)" A state is **safe** if there exists a **safe sequence** of processes $\langle P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n \rangle$ such that: For each $i$, the resources $P_i$ still needs can be satisfied by the **currently available** resources plus those held by $P_1, \ldots, P_{i-1}$. ???+ info "Key facts" - **Safe state** ≠ **no deadlock** — every safe state is deadlock-free, but some unsafe states are also deadlock-free. - A safe state **guarantees** that all processes can finish — by following the safe sequence. - An unsafe state **may or may not** deadlock — depends on future requests. !!! warning "The conservative nature of avoidance" Avoidance may refuse a request even though granting it would not deadlock — because it cannot **guarantee** no future deadlock. This is the price of safety.

docs.title: 5.7 — Banker's Algorithm
docs.text:
Data structures (Silberschatz §7.5.3)

For \(n\) processes and \(m\) resource types:

Structure Dimensions Meaning Available \(m\) Free resources Max \(n \times m\) Max demand per process Allocation \(n \times m\) Current allocation Need \(n \times m\) \(Max - Allocation\) ???+ note "The safety algorithm" 
Work = Available
Finish = [false, false, ..., false]

while (exists i with Finish[i] == false and Need[i] <= Work):
    Work = Work + Allocation[i]
    Finish[i] = true

return all(Finish)
???+ note "The resource-request algorithm" When $P_i$ requests `Request[i]`: 1. If `Request[i] > Need[i]`, error. 2. If `Request[i] > Available`, $P_i$ must wait. 3. **Pretend** to allocate: `Available -= Request`, `Allocation[i] += Request`, `Need[i] -= Request`. 4. Run the safety algorithm. 5. If **safe**, grant; else **roll back** and make $P_i$ wait.

docs.title: Worked example 5.2 — Banker's algorithm safety check
docs.text:
Problem:

System with resource types A, B, C, totals (10, 5, 7).

Process Allocation Max Need P0 (0,1,0) (7,5,3) (7,4,3) P1 (2,0,0) (3,2,2) (1,2,2) P2 (3,0,2) (9,0,2) (6,0,0) P3 (2,1,1) (2,2,2) (0,1,1) P4 (0,0,2) (4,3,3) (4,3,1) ???+ note "**Step 1 — available.**" Total allocated: $(0+2+3+2+0, 1+0+0+1+0, 0+0+2+1+2) = (7, 2, 5)$. Available = $(10,5,7) - (7,2,5) = (3, 3, 2)$. ??? info "**Step 2 — find a satisfying process.**" `Work = (3, 3, 2)`. Which process has `Need ≤ Work`? - P1 needs (1, 2, 2) ≤ (3, 3, 2) ✓. **Finish P1.** - `Work = (3, 3, 2) + (2, 0, 0) = (5, 3, 2)`. ??? info "**Step 3 — continue.**" - P3 needs (0, 1, 1) ≤ (5, 3, 2) ✓. **Finish P3.** - `Work = (5, 3, 2) + (2, 1, 1) = (7, 4, 3)`. - P4 needs (4, 3, 1) ≤ (7, 4, 3) ✓. **Finish P4.** - `Work = (7, 4, 3) + (0, 0, 2) = (7, 4, 5)`. - P0 needs (7, 4, 3) ≤ (7, 4, 5) ✓. **Finish P0.** - `Work = (7, 4, 5) + (0, 1, 0) = (7, 5, 5)`. - P2 needs (6, 0, 0) ≤ (7, 5, 5) ✓. **Finish P2.** ??? success "**Conclusion.**" **Safe sequence: ⟨P1, P3, P4, P0, P2⟩.** The system is in a **safe state**. Any process can now request up to its Need, as long as the resulting state remains safe.

docs.title: Worked example 5.3 — Banker's algorithm request
docs.text:
Problem:

In the safe state above, P1 requests (1, 0, 2).

???+ note "**Step 1 — validate.**" `Request[P1] = (1, 0, 2) ≤ Need[P1] = (1, 2, 2)` ✓. `Request[P1] = (1, 0, 2) ≤ Available = (3, 3, 2)` ✓. ??? info "**Step 2 — pretend allocation.**" - Available = (3, 3, 2) − (1, 0, 2) = (2, 3, 0). - Allocation[P1] = (2, 0, 0) + (1, 0, 2) = (3, 0, 2). - Need[P1] = (1, 2, 2) − (1, 0, 2) = (0, 2, 0). ??? info "**Step 3 — run safety algorithm.**" `Work = (2, 3, 0)`. - P1 needs (0, 2, 0) ≤ (2, 3, 0) ✓. Finish. `Work = (5, 3, 2)`. - P3 needs (0, 1, 1) ≤ (5, 3, 2) ✓. Finish. `Work = (7, 4, 3)`. - P4 needs (4, 3, 1) ≤ (7, 4, 3) ✓. Finish. `Work = (7, 4, 5)`. - P0 needs (7, 4, 3) ≤ (7, 4, 5) ✓. Finish. `Work = (7, 5, 5)`. - P2 needs (6, 0, 0) ≤ (7, 5, 5) ✓. Finish. All done. ??? success "**Conclusion.**" Request is **safe** → **granted**. P1 now has (3, 0, 2), still needs (0, 2, 0), and the system remains in a safe state.

docs.title: 5.8 — Deadlock Detection
docs.text:
The idea

If prevention and avoidance are too costly, allow deadlock and detect it periodically.

???+ note "Single instance per resource — wait-for graph" Build a graph with processes as nodes. Edge $P_i \to P_j$ if $P_i$ waits for a resource held by $P_j$. **Deadlock exists iff the wait-for graph has a cycle.** ???+ note "Multiple instances — detection algorithm" Variant of the safety algorithm: 
Work = Available
Finish[i] = false if Allocation[i] > 0 else true

while (exists i with Finish[i] == false and Request[i] <= Work):
    Work = Work + Allocation[i]
    Finish[i] = true

Deadlock exists iff some Finish[i] == false.
!!! warning "Detection cost" Running the detection algorithm on every request is **$O(n^2 m)$** — expensive. Real systems run it periodically (e.g., every minute) or when the CPU is idle.

docs.title: Worked example 5.4 — Wait-for graph
docs.text:
Problem:

P1 holds R1, requests R2.
P2 holds R2, requests R3.
P3 holds R3, requests R1.
???+ note "**Step 1 — draw the wait-for graph.**" 
P1 ──► P2 ──► P3 ──► P1
??? info "**Step 2 — check for a cycle.**" P1 → P2 → P3 → P1. **Cycle exists.** ??? success "**Conclusion.**" **Deadlock** in processes P1, P2, P3. !!! tip "Cycle detection is fast" Depth-first search on the wait-for graph is $O(V + E)$ — cheap enough to run on every request in single-instance systems.

docs.title: 5.9 — Deadlock Recovery
docs.text: Three approaches Approach Cost Risk Process termination Kill processes Loss of work Resource preemption Take resources Rollback needed Process rollback Restore checkpoint Checkpoint overhead   ???+ note "Which process to terminate?"     - **Kill all** deadlocked processes — simple but drastic.     - **Kill one at a time** until cycle broken — better but slow.     - **Priorities:** low priority, least work, fewest resources.     ???+ note "Resource preemption issues"     1. **Victim selection** — which process to preempt?     2. **Rollback** — restore the victim to a safe state.     3. **Starvation** — a process may be preempted repeatedly. Fix: count preemptions, refuse to preempt a process more than $k$ times.

docs.title: 5.10 — Comparison: Prevention vs Avoidance vs Detection
docs.text: The trade-off Aspect Prevention Avoidance Detection Overhead Low (static rules) Medium (run safety on every request) Low (periodic detection) Resource utilisation Low (over-conservative) Medium High Deadlock possible? No No Yes, until detected Best for Small, static systems Batch systems with known max demands Large dynamic systems   !!! tip "What real systems use"     - **Linux/Windows:** **Ostrich algorithm** — ignore deadlock, rely on the user to kill stuck processes.     - **Databases:** **Timeout-based** — abort long transactions.     - **Safety-critical:** **Prevention** — statically prove no deadlock possible.     - **Distributed systems:** **Detection + recovery** — no global knowledge of resources.     ???+ note "The ostrich algorithm"     "Put your head in the sand and pretend the problem doesn't exist." Modern general-purpose OSes do this — deadlocks are rare, and the cost of prevention (low utilisation) exceeds the cost of occasional user intervention.

docs.title: 5.11 — Deadlock in Practice
docs.text: Real-world deadlock scenarios Domain Example Databases Two transactions lock rows in opposite order OS kernels Two drivers acquire two mutexes in opposite order Distributed systems Two nodes wait for network messages from each other Web servers Two requests wait for each other's database locks   !!! tip "Prevention in practice"     - **Lock ordering** — all code acquires locks in a global order.     - **Try-lock with timeout** — never wait indefinitely.     - **Deadlock detection services** — some databases monitor and abort cycles automatically.

docs.title: Chapter 5 — key takeaways
docs.text: **1.** A **deadlock** requires all four **Coffman conditions**: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no-preemption, circular wait.     **2.** The **resource allocation graph** shows deadlock visually — a cycle is **sufficient** for single-instance resources but only **necessary** for multi-instance.     **3.** **Prevention** breaks one condition — cheapest (no deadlock) but lowest utilisation. **Circular-wait prevention** (lock ordering) is the practical choice.     **4.** **Avoidance** (Banker's algorithm) requires knowing max demands and checking every request for **safety**.     **5.** **Detection** uses wait-for graphs (single instance) or a detection algorithm (multi-instance). Cheaper than prevention but allows temporary deadlock.     **6.** **Recovery** by process termination or resource preemption. Preemption must avoid starvation.     **7.** Real systems often use the **ostrich algorithm** — deadlock is rare; user intervention is acceptable.

docs.title: Next — Chapter 6
docs.text:
Memory Management.

- **Contiguous allocation** and fragmentation. - **Paging** — page tables, TLB, multi-level tables. - **Segmentation** — logical segments. - **Virtual memory** — demand paging, page faults. - **Page replacement** — FIFO, LRU, Optimal, Clock. - **Thrashing** and working set. Chapter 5 showed what happens when processes compete for **finite** resources. Chapter 6 shows the biggest finite resource of all — **memory**.

docs.text: 1. Explain **address binding** (compile, load, execution) and the role of the **MMU**.     2. Distinguish **fixed**, **variable**, and **buddy-system** partitioning; identify fragmentation types.     3. Translate a **virtual address** to a **physical address** in a paging system, using the **TLB**.     4. Compare **paging** and **segmentation**.     5. Trace **page-replacement algorithms** (FIFO, LRU, Optimal, Clock) on a reference string.     6. Define and detect **thrashing**; use the **working-set** model.

docs.title: 6.1 — The Memory Hierarchy
docs.text:
Registers         ← CPU
    │
L1 Cache          ~32 KB
    │
L2 Cache          ~256 KB
    │
L3 Cache          ~8 MB
    │
Main Memory       ~8–32 GB
    │
Disk (SSD/HDD)    ~TB
!!! tip "The management problem" Each process wants **all the memory it needs**, at high speed, isolated from other processes. The OS and MMU together provide the illusion of **more memory** and **private memory** — using caches, paging, and virtual memory.

docs.title: 6.2 — Address Binding
docs.text: Three times When Binding Consequence Compile time Absolute addresses Program must load at a fixed address Load time Relocatable addresses Program can load anywhere, fixed at load Execution time Virtual addresses Program can move during execution   ???+ info "Modern systems use execution-time binding"     Every load/store instruction computes a **virtual address**, which the **MMU** translates to a **physical address** on every memory access. This enables:     - **Paging** — page can be anywhere in physical memory.     - **Swapping** — page can be on disk and brought in on demand.     - **Protection** — page permissions enforced by the MMU.

docs.title: 6.3 — The Memory Management Unit
docs.text:
The MMU's job

Translate every virtual address to a physical address.

CPU ──► Virtual address ──► MMU ──► Physical address ──► Memory
                              │
                              └── consults page table
???+ info "Two mappings" - **Paging** — virtual page number + offset → physical frame number + offset. - **Segmentation** — segment number + offset → base + offset. !!! tip "The MMU is hardware" The page-table walk is implemented in silicon. Without the MMU, every memory access would need an OS system call — 1000× slower.

docs.title: 6.4 — Fixed Partitioning
docs.text:
The idea

Divide memory into fixed-size partitions. Each process gets one partition.

Memory:
┌──────────┐
│ Part 1   │  ← process A (fits)
├──────────┤
│ Part 2   │  ← process B (fits)
├──────────┤
│ Part 3   │  ← EMPTY (no process of this size)
├──────────┤
│ Part 4   │  ← process C (fits)
└──────────┘
???+ warning "Internal fragmentation" A process **smaller** than its partition wastes the remainder. If partition = 100 MB and process = 30 MB, 70 MB is wasted. ???+ info "How bad?" In the worst case, up to 50% of memory is wasted. This is why fixed partitioning is rarely used today (except in embedded systems).

docs.title: 6.5 — Variable Partitioning
docs.text:
The idea

Allocate each process exactly the memory it needs. Partitions are variable-sized.

???+ warning "External fragmentation" Free memory is scattered in small **holes** between allocations. Even if the total free memory is enough, **no single hole** may be large enough. ???+ note "Allocation strategies" | Strategy | Behaviour | |---|---| | **First-fit** | First hole large enough | | **Best-fit** | Smallest hole large enough | | **Worst-fit** | Largest hole | ???+ info "Fixes for external fragmentation" - **Compaction** — shuffle memory to coalesce holes. Expensive. - **Paging** — eliminate the requirement for contiguity (Section 6.7). - **Segmentation** — still has fragmentation but with logical meaning.

docs.title: Worked example 6.1 — First-fit vs best-fit
docs.text:
Problem:

Memory holes: [100, 500, 200, 300, 600]. Requests in order: [212, 417, 112, 426].

???+ note "**First-fit.**" - 212 → hole 500 (splits to 288). Holes: [100, 288, 200, 300, 600]. - 417 → hole 600 (splits to 183). Holes: [100, 288, 200, 300, 183]. - 112 → hole 288 (splits to 176). Holes: [100, 176, 200, 300, 183]. - 426 → no hole ≥ 426. **Fails.** ??? info "**Best-fit.**" - 212 → hole 300 (splits to 88). Holes: [100, 500, 200, 88, 600]. - 417 → hole 500 (splits to 83). Holes: [100, 83, 200, 88, 600]. - 112 → hole 200 (splits to 88). Holes: [100, 83, 88, 88, 600]. - 426 → hole 600 (splits to 174). Holes: [100, 83, 88, 88, 174]. **All succeed.** ??? success "**Observation.**" Best-fit does more work (searches all holes) but produces **smaller leftover holes** and **fewer failures**. First-fit is faster but more likely to leave large unusable holes.

docs.title: 6.6 — Buddy System
docs.text:
The idea

Memory is allocated in power-of-two blocks. A request is rounded up to the next power of two. If unavailable, a larger block is split in half (buddies).

???+ note "Example: request 50 KB" - Round up to 64 KB. - If no 64 KB block, take a 128 KB block and split into two 64 KB buddies. - If no 128 KB block, split 256 KB, etc. ???+ info "Finding a buddy" If a block is at address $A$ and has size $2^k$, its buddy is at address $A \oplus 2^k$ (XOR). ???+ note "Pros and cons" - **Fast allocation and coalescing** — buddy find is O(1). - **Internal fragmentation** — rounded up to power of two → up to 50% waste.

docs.title: 6.7 — Paging
docs.text:
The idea

Divide physical memory into fixed-size frames (e.g., 4 KB). Divide logical memory into same-size pages. Pages can go in any frame — no contiguity needed.

???+ note "Address translation" 
Virtual address:
┌─────────────┬────────┐
│ page number │ offset │
└─────────────┴────────┘
       │           │
       ▼           │
┌─────────────┐    │
│ page table  │    │
└─────────────┘    │
       │           │
       ▼           ▼
┌─────────────┬────────┐
│frame number │ offset │
└─────────────┴────────┘
Physical address
???+ success "Paging eliminates external fragmentation" Every page fits in every frame. Free frames can be reused without coalescing. ???+ warning "Internal fragmentation remains" The **last page** of a process may be partially filled — waste up to (page_size − 1) bytes. With 4 KB pages, average waste is 2 KB per process.

docs.title: 6.8 — The Page Table
docs.text:
Definition

The page table maps page numbers to frame numbers. One entry per page of the process.

???+ note "Page table entry (PTE)" 
┌─────┬─────┬──────────────────┐
│ Valid│ Dirty│ Frame number     │
└─────┴─────┴──────────────────┘
- **Valid bit** — is the page in memory? - **Dirty bit** — has the page been written? - **Reference bit** — has the page been accessed? (for LRU/Clock) - **Protection bits** — read/write/execute. !!! warning "Where is the page table stored?" In **physical memory** (not in a register). Every memory access requires reading a PTE — **doubling** the memory traffic. This is why the TLB exists.

docs.title: 6.9 — The TLB
docs.text:
Translation Lookaside Buffer

A small associative cache of recent page-table entries. On a TLB hit, translation is fast; on a miss, the page table is consulted.

???+ note "Effective access time (EAT)" $$ \text{EAT} = \alpha \cdot (t_{\text{TLB}} + t_{\text{mem}}) + (1-\alpha) \cdot (t_{\text{TLB}} + 2 t_{\text{mem}}) $$ where $\alpha$ is the TLB hit rate. ???+ info "Typical numbers" - $t_{\text{TLB}} = 1$ ns, $t_{\text{mem}} = 100$ ns, $\alpha = 0.99$. - EAT = $0.99 \times 101 + 0.01 \times 201 = 99.99 + 2.01 = 102$ ns. A 1% TLB miss rate **doubles** the memory access time — TLB hit rate matters enormously. !!! tip "TLB flushing on context switch" When the OS switches to a different process, the TLB entries become invalid — they belong to the old process's address space. Modern CPUs use **ASIDs** (address space IDs) to tag TLB entries, avoiding the flush.

docs.title: Worked example 6.2 — Paging translation
docs.text:
Problem:

Page size = 4 KB (offset = 12 bits). Virtual address = 0x00002A3F. Page table:

Page # Frame # 0 5 1 3 2 8

Find the physical address.

???+ note "**Step 1 — split the address.**" `0x00002A3F` = binary `0000 0000 0000 0000 0010 1010 0011 1111`. - Offset (low 12 bits) = `0xA3F` = 2623. - Page number = `0x2` = 2. ??? info "**Step 2 — look up the page table.**" Page 2 → frame 8. ??? success "**Step 3 — assemble the physical address.**" Physical = frame 8 × 4 KB + offset 2623 = 32768 + 2623 = **35391 = 0x8A3F**. ???+ info "**Sanity check.**" The physical address should have the same low 12 bits as the virtual address (`A3F`), with the frame number in the high bits. ✓

docs.title: 6.10 — Multi-Level Page Tables
docs.text:
The problem

For a 32-bit address space with 4 KB pages: \(2^{20}\) pages = ~1M entries per page table = 4 MB per process. For 1000 processes, that's 4 GB just for page tables.

???+ note "The solution — multi-level page tables" Split the page table into a tree. Only the levels that are actually used need to be allocated. 
Virtual address:  | PGD | PUD | PMD | PTE | offset |
                    │
                    ▼
                Page global directory
                    │
                    ▼
                Page upper directory
                    │
                    ▼
                Page middle directory
                    │
                    ▼
                Page table entry
???+ info "Typical x86-64 layout" - 4 levels of page tables. - Each level uses 9 bits of the 48-bit virtual address. - 12 bits offset. - Total: 4 × 9 + 12 = 48 bits. !!! warning "Multi-level tables are slower" Each level of the tree is one memory access. A 4-level walk needs **4 memory accesses** per TLB miss. This is why TLB hit rate is so critical.

docs.title: 6.11 — Segmentation
docs.text:
The idea

Divide the program into logical segments — code, data, stack, heap — each with its own base and limit.

???+ note "Address translation" Segment number + offset → segment table lookup → physical address. ???+ note "Pros" - **Matches programmer's view** of memory. - **Natural protection** — code segment read-only, stack writable. - **Sharing** — two processes share the same code segment. ???+ note "Cons" - **External fragmentation** — segments are variable-size. - **Complex hardware** — segment table plus offset check. !!! tip "Paging vs segmentation" | Aspect | Paging | Segmentation | |---|---|---| | Size | Fixed | Variable | | Internal frag | Yes (last page) | No | | External frag | No | Yes | | Programmer view | Invisible | Matches structure | | Modern use | Yes (with segmentation) | Mostly historical |

docs.title: 6.12 — Virtual Memory
docs.text:
The idea

Give each process a virtual address space larger than physical memory. Only the currently used pages are in memory; the rest are on disk.

???+ note "Demand paging" A page is loaded **on demand** — when the process accesses it, and only then. If the page is not in memory, a **page fault** occurs. ???+ note "The page-fault handler" 1. Trap to kernel (page fault). 2. Find a **free frame** (or evict one). 3. Read the page from disk. 4. Update the page table (mark valid). 5. Restart the faulting instruction. !!! tip "Why virtual memory works" Programs exhibit **locality** — at any moment, they access a small subset of their pages (the working set). The OS keeps this working set in memory and swaps the rest to disk.

docs.title: 6.13 — Page Replacement Algorithms
docs.text:
The problem

Memory is full. A new page must be loaded. Which page to evict?

???+ note "The four classic algorithms" | Algorithm | Rule | Optimal? | |---|---|---| | **FIFO** |

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text: 1. Describe a **file** — attributes, operations, access methods.     2. Compare **directory structures**: linear, hash, tree, DAG.     3. Compare **file allocation methods**: contiguous, linked, indexed.     4. Trace a lookup through a **Unix inode**, including indirect blocks.     5. Explain **free-space management** (bitmap, linked list, grouping).     6. Describe **journaling** and why it prevents file-system corruption.

docs.title: 7.1 — What is a File?
docs.text:
Definition (Silberschatz §10.1)

A file is a named, persistent collection of related information stored on secondary storage.

???+ note "File attributes" | Attribute | Meaning | |---|---| | **Name** | Human-readable identifier | | **Identifier** | Unique internal tag (usually an inode number) | | **Type** | Regular, directory, symbolic link, device | | **Location** | Pointer to disk blocks | | **Size** | Current length | | **Protection** | Read/write/execute permissions | | **Timestamps** | Created, modified, accessed | | **Owner** | User, group | ???+ note "File operations" `create`, `open`, `read`, `write`, `seek`, `close`, `delete`, `truncate`, `append`.

docs.title: 7.2 — Access Methods
docs.text:
Sequential access

Read/write bytes in order. The next byte is always after the previous one.

Best for: logs, streaming media, tape.

???+ note "Direct (random) access" Read/write at any position by specifying the offset. 
read(file, offset=1024, buffer, size=100)
**Best for:** databases, executable files, anything requiring seek. ???+ note "Indexed access" An **index** maps keys to byte offsets. Allows lookup by key. !!! tip "Modern OSes support all three" POSIX `read()`/`write()` operate on the file's current position. `lseek()` changes the position, enabling direct access. `open()` returns a file descriptor with a **current offset** — a per-fd cursor. --- ## 7.3 — Directory Structures ???+ note "What is a directory?" A directory is a **special file** that maps names to inodes. The kernel uses it to resolve pathnames. ???+ note "Four structures" | Structure | Lookup | Example | |---|---|---| | **Linear list** | $O(n)$ scan | Old FAT | | **Hash table** | $O(1)$ average | ext4 (directory hash) | | **Tree (B-tree)** | $O(\log n)$ | NTFS, XFS | | **DAG** | $O(1)$ per link | Unix hard links | ???+ note "Unix hard links and symbolic links" - **Hard link** — another name for the same inode. Two directory entries point to the same inode. Deleting one does not delete the file. - **Symbolic link (soft link)** — a file whose content is the path of another file. Deleting the target breaks the link. !!! warning "Hard links and directories" Modern Unix restricts hard links to files (not directories) — allowing them would create cycles in the directory tree, requiring garbage collection. --- ## 7.4 — Allocation Methods: The Core Trade-off ???+ note "The question" A file needs $N$ blocks. Which disk blocks does it get, and how does the file system find them? ???+ note "Three methods" | Method | Sequential access | Random access | Space overhead | |---|---|---|---| | **Contiguous** | Excellent | Excellent | None | | **Linked** | Good | Poor | One pointer per block | | **Indexed** | Good | Excellent | One index block | !!! tip "The trade-off triangle" - **Performance** (contiguous wins). - **Fragmentation resistance** (linked wins). - **Direct access** (contiguous and indexed win). --- ## 7.5 — Contiguous Allocation ???+ note "The idea" Each file occupies a **contiguous block** of disk. 
File A: blocks 10-19
File B: blocks 20-29
File C: blocks 30-32
???+ note "Pros" - **Fast sequential access** — one seek to the start, then linear. - **Fast direct access** — one seek to `start + offset`. - **No per-block overhead** — just start and length. ???+ note "Cons" - **External fragmentation** — as files grow and shrink, free space splits into holes. - **Growth is painful** — a growing file may need to be **moved** to a new contiguous region. - **Compaction** required to reclaim large free regions. !!! warning "Contiguous allocation is rare today" Only used in read-only file systems (CD-ROM, ISO 9660) and in specific modern uses (extent-based allocation in ext4, which is contiguous but with extents). The growth problem killed pure contiguous allocation for general-purpose FS. --- ## 7.6 — Linked Allocation ???+ note "The idea" Each file is a **linked list of blocks**. The first block is a pointer; each block contains a pointer to the next. 
Block 10: [data | ptr to 20]
Block 20: [data | ptr to 35]
Block 35: [data | ptr to 42]
Block 42: [data | NULL]
???+ note "Pros" - **No external fragmentation** — any free block can join any list. - **File can grow** — append a block, update the tail's pointer. ???+ note "Cons" - **Direct access is slow** — to reach byte 1,000,000, walk the chain. - **Pointer overhead** — 4 bytes per block (or more). - **Fragile** — a corrupted pointer loses the rest of the file. ???+ tip "FAT (File Allocation Table)" DOS's solution: store **all** pointers in a separate **File Allocation Table** at the start of the disk. Each FAT entry is one disk block. Direct access still requires walking the FAT, but the FAT is cached in memory. --- ## 7.7 — Indexed Allocation ???+ note "The idea" Each file has an **index block** — an array of pointers to the file's data blocks. 
Inode:
  index_block → [data_block_1, data_block_2, ..., data_block_N]
???+ note "Pros" - **Direct access is fast** — index gives O(1) access to any block. - **No external fragmentation** — any free block can be a data block. ???+ note "Cons" - **Index block overhead** — for small files, an entire block (4 KB) is reserved but mostly unused. - **Multi-level index required for large files** — the Unix inode uses single, double, and triple indirect. !!! tip "Modern file systems use hybrid schemes" ext4 uses **extents** — a single entry describes a contiguous range of blocks. This gives the speed of contiguous allocation with the flexibility of indexing. --- ## 7.8 — The Unix Inode ???+ note "The inode structure" Each file has an **inode** with metadata and 15 pointers: 
Inode:
  mode, owner, size, timestamps, ...
  direct[0..11]          12 direct pointers
  single_indirect[1]     1 pointer to a block of 1024 pointers
  double_indirect[1]     1 pointer to a block of 1024 single-indirect blocks
  triple_indirect[1]     1 pointer to a block of 1024 double-indirect blocks
???+ note "File size limits (4 KB blocks, 4 B pointers)" | Level | Coverage | |---|---| | Direct (12) | $12 \times 4\,\text{KB} = 48\,\text{KB}$ | | Single indirect | $1024 \times 4\,\text{KB} = 4\,\text{MB}$ | | Double indirect | $1024^2 \times 4\,\text{KB} = 4\,\text{GB}$ | | Triple indirect | $1024^3 \times 4\,\text{KB} = 4\,\text{TB}$ | ???+ success "The genius of the inode" - **Small files** — accessed via direct pointers, no extra blocks touched. - **Large files** — accessed via indirect pointers, scaling to 4 TB. - **Flexible** — the same inode structure handles files from 1 byte to 4 TB. --- ## Worked example 7.1 — Trace a file offset in the inode !!! tip "Problem:" A file is 100 KB. Block size = 4 KB. Where do the following offsets live? ???+ note "**Offset 0 (first byte).**" Block 0. Direct pointer 0. ??? info "**Offset 24,000 (≈ 5.9 blocks).**" Block 5. Direct pointer 5. ??? info "**Offset 100,000 (≈ 24.4 blocks).**" Block 24. That's > 12 (direct limit) and < 1024 (single indirect limit). Lookup: - Read `single_indirect[0]` → indirect block. - Read indirect[24 − 12] = indirect[12] → data block 24. ??? info "**File size 10 MB.**" Block 2500 — within single indirect (up to 4 MB) and double indirect (up to 4 GB). Lookup: - Read `single_indirect[0]` → indirect block. - Then `double_indirect[0]` → second indirect block. - Then `[2500 − 1024 − 12]` → data block. ??? success "**Trade-off.** The farther into the file, the more indirect blocks the OS must read. Small files are fast; large files are still OK, just with a few extra indirections." --- ## 7.9 — Free Space Management ???+ note "The question" The OS must know which blocks are free. Which data structure tracks this? ???+ note "Three approaches" | Method | Structure | Trade-off | |---|---|---| | **Bitmap** | One bit per block | Fast lookup, large space | | **Linked list** | Linked list of free blocks | Small space, slow scan | | **Grouping** | Block of block addresses | Between the two | ???+ note "Bitmap" 
1011000111000101 1101 ...
- Bit = 1 → free. - Bit = 0 → allocated. For a 1 TB disk with 4 KB blocks ($2^{28}$ blocks): bitmap = $2^{28}$ bits = 32 MB. Small relative to disk size. ???+ note "Linked list" 
free_list_head → block 5 → block 12 → block 19 → ... → NULL
- **Space:** small (one pointer per free block). - **Lookup:** $O(\text{free})$ — cannot tell if a specific block is free without walking. !!! tip "Ext4 uses a hybrid" Ext4 uses a **bitmap** for the inode table and **extent-based free space management** for data blocks. Best of both worlds. --- ## 7.10 — Journaling ???+ note "The problem" A power failure during a write can leave the file system **inconsistent** — a pointer updated but the data not written, or a directory entry pointing to a freed block. ???+ note "The journaling solution" Before making any change, **write it to a journal** first. Once the journal entry is on disk, the change is safe — it can be replayed after a crash. ???+ note "The three-step protocol" 1. **Journal write** — write the intended change to the journal area. 2. **Commit** — write a commit record to the journal. 3. **Checkpoint** — apply the change to the actual file-system data. If a crash occurs before step 2, the journal is ignored. If after step 2, the journal is replayed on reboot. ???+ info "Journaling modes" | Mode | What is journaled | Speed | Consistency | |---|---|---|---| | **Journal** | Data + metadata | Slowest | Strongest | | **Ordered** (default ext4) | Metadata (data written first) | Medium | Good | | **Writeback** | Metadata only | Fastest | Weakest | !!! tip "Journaling ≠ backup" Journaling ensures **consistency** — the file system is always in a valid state after a crash. It does not protect against accidental deletion, corruption, or ransomware. Backup is a separate concern. --- ## Worked example 7.2 — Journal replay !!! tip "Problem:" A crash occurs after the journal has a "commit" record for a new file, but the directory entry has not yet been written. What happens on reboot? ???+ note "**Step 1 — scan the journal.**" The file system finds the journal entry with a valid commit record. ??? info "**Step 2 — replay.**" The journal entry describes the intended operation. The file system re-applies it — creating the directory entry that wasn't written before the crash. ??? success "**Result.**" The file exists. The file system is consistent. If the journal entry had **no** commit record, it would be ignored (the file would not exist — as if the crash happened before the create was requested). !!! tip "The order matters" Data must be written to disk **before** the journal is committed (in ordered mode). Otherwise, after replay, the journal points to a data block that was never written — corrupt. --- ## 7.11 — File System Performance ???+ note "The buffer cache" The OS caches recently accessed disk blocks in memory. A read that hits the cache avoids a disk access — 100,000× faster. ???+ note "Performance optimizations" | Technique | Benefit | |---|---| | **Buffer cache** | Avoids disk reads for hot data | | **Read-ahead** | Prefetches sequential blocks | | **Journaling** | Fast recovery after crash | | **Extents** (ext4, XFS) | Contiguous allocation for large files | | **Delayed allocation** | Batches small writes into large ones | ???+ note "The writeback problem" Write-back caching improves performance but delays durability. `fsync(fd)` forces a write to disk — essential for databases and journals. !!! tip "The small-file problem" Many small files (e.g., a git repo) exercise the inode allocator and directory structure heavily. Filesystems like **XFS** and **btrfs** optimize for this; ext4 is decent but not ideal. --- ## 7.12 — Modern File Systems ???+ note "A brief comparison" | FS | Journaled | CoW | Compression | Typical use | |---|---|---|---|---| | **ext4** | Yes | No | No | Linux default | | **XFS** | Yes | No | No | Large files, servers | | **btrfs** | CoW | Yes | Yes | Snapshots, containers | | **ZFS** | CoW | Yes | Yes | Storage servers, NAS | | **NTFS** | Yes | No | Yes | Windows | | **APFS** | CoW | Yes | Yes | macOS, iOS | !!! tip "Copy-on-write (CoW) file systems" Btrfs and ZFS never overwrite data — they write new blocks and update pointers. This gives: - **Snapshots** for free — just record the current root pointer. - **Cheap clones** — share blocks until modified. - **Atomic updates** — no half-written state. --- ## Chapter 7 — key takeaways **1.** A **file** is a named, persistent collection of bytes. Attributes include name, size, timestamps, and protection. **2.** **Access methods**: sequential, direct, indexed. Modern OSes support all three via `lseek`. **3.** **Directory structures**: linear (slow), hash (fast), tree (scales), DAG (Unix links). **4.** **Allocation methods**: contiguous (fast, fragmentation), linked (flexible, slow), indexed (good compromise, inode). **5.** The **Unix inode** combines direct and indirect pointers to handle files from bytes to terabytes. **6.** **Free-space management**: bitmap (fast, large), linked list (small, slow). **7.** **Journaling** ensures consistency after crash — write intent to journal, then apply. **8.** Modern file systems (btrfs, ZFS) use **copy-on-write** for snapshots and atomicity. --- ## Next — Chapter 8 **I/O Management.** - **I/O hardware**: controllers, buses, device registers. - **Four I/O software layers**. - **Programmed I/O**, **interrupt-driven**, **DMA**. - **Disk scheduling**: FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK. - **Disk caching** and **buffering**. Chapter 7 managed **persistent** storage. Chapter 8 manages the **mechanisms** that move data between devices and memory.

docs.text: 1. Classify I/O devices (**block**, **character**, **network**) and their interfaces.     2. Describe the **four layers** of I/O software.     3. Compare **programmed I/O**, **interrupt-driven I/O**, and **DMA**.     4. Trace a **disk-scheduling** algorithm (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK) on a queue.     5. Explain **buffering**, **caching**, and **spooling**.

docs.title: 8.1 — I/O Device Classes
docs.text: Three classes Class Examples Transfer unit Access Block HDD, SSD, USB drive Block (512 B – 4 KB) Random Character Keyboard, serial Byte Sequential Network Ethernet, Wi-Fi Packet Streaming   ???+ note "Device controllers"     Each device has a **controller** — an embedded processor that:     - Translates CPU commands to device actions.     - Manages the protocol (SATA, NVMe, USB, PCIe).     - Buffers data.     - Reports status (ready, busy, error).     ???+ note "Device registers"     | Register | Purpose |     |---|---|     | **Data** | Holds the transferred data |     | **Status** | Ready, busy, error, done |     | **Control** | Start, direction, interrupt enable |     !!! tip "Memory-mapped vs isolated I/O"     - **Memory-mapped** — device registers appear at memory addresses; accessed via normal `load`/`store`.     - **Isolated** — separate address space; needs dedicated `IN`/`OUT` instructions (x86).      Memory-mapped is more common in modern systems — uniform addressing, works with any memory instruction.

docs.title: 8.2 — The Four I/O Software Layers
docs.text:
┌────────────────────────────────┐
│  User-space I/O library        │  printf, fread, ...
├────────────────────────────────┤
│  OS-independent I/O software   │  buffering, spooling, names
├────────────────────────────────┤
│  Device drivers                │  device-specific code
├────────────────────────────────┤
│  Interrupt handlers            │  hardware → OS
└────────────────────────────────┘
???+ note "What each layer does" | Layer | Responsibility | |---|---| | **User-space library** | Format I/O, call syscalls | | **OS-independent** | Buffering, caching, naming, protection | | **Device drivers** | Talk to the controller | | **Interrupt handlers** | Respond to device events | !!! tip "Device drivers are ~70% of the Linux kernel" Linux has ~30 million lines of code, of which ~20 million are device drivers. This is the practical cost of supporting thousands of hardware devices.

docs.title: 8.3 — Programmed I/O (Polling)
8.4 — Interrupt-Driven I/O
docs.text:
The algorithm
  1. CPU issues a read command.
  2. CPU does other work.
  3. Device raises an interrupt when ready.
  4. CPU runs the interrupt handler, which reads the data.
???+ note "Trace" | Time | CPU | Device | |---|---|---| | 0 | issues command, returns to work | starts | | 1–999 | runs other processes | working | | 1000 | interrupted | raises IRQ | | 1001 | runs handler, reads data | — | | 1002 | resumes | — | ???+ note "Interrupt overhead" - **Context save/restore:** ~100 ns. - **Handler code:** depends on the device. - **Total:** ~1–10 µs per interrupt. ???+ warning "Interrupt overload" A 10 Gbps network card receives ~15 million packets per second. If each packet causes an interrupt, the CPU is overwhelmed. Solutions: - **Interrupt coalescing** — batch many packets into one interrupt. - **NAPI** (Linux) — switch to polling under high load. - **DMA** — transfer batches, one interrupt per batch.

docs.title: 8.5 — Direct Memory Access (DMA)
docs.text:
The algorithm
  1. CPU programs the DMA controller: source, destination, length, direction.
  2. CPU continues execution.
  3. DMA controller takes ownership of the bus and transfers data.
  4. DMA controller raises an interrupt when done.
???+ note "Trace" | Time | CPU | DMA controller | Device | |---|---|---|---| | 0 | sets up DMA | idle | idle | | 1 | runs other work | transfers blocks | streaming | | ... | ... | ... | ... | | 5000 | interrupted | done | done | | 5001 | acknowledges | idle | idle | ???+ note "Cost analysis" - Setup: ~1 µs (CPU programs DMA registers). - Transfer: no CPU involvement. - Completion: ~1 µs (interrupt). Total CPU time: **~2 µs per transfer**, regardless of transfer size. ???+ warning "Cycle stealing" The DMA controller **competes with the CPU** for the memory bus. During DMA transfers, the CPU's own memory accesses are slowed. Modern systems minimise this with: - **Direct Cache Access (DCA)** — DMA writes go through the CPU's cache. - **IOMMU** — separates device memory access from CPU memory access.

docs.title: 8.6 — Comparison of I/O Mechanisms
docs.text: The three approaches Aspect Programmed Interrupt DMA CPU per byte Yes No No CPU during transfer Busy-wait Free Free Per-transfer overhead High Medium Low Throughput Low Medium High Complexity Simple Moderate Complex Best for Simple embedded Slow devices Bulk transfers   !!! tip "Which to choose"     - **Keyboard, mouse:** interrupt.     - **Disk, network, USB:** DMA.     - **Simple microcontroller with no interrupt controller:** polling.

docs.title: Worked example 8.1 — Disk I/O time
docs.text:
Problem:

A disk has: - Average seek time: 9 ms. - Rotation speed: 7200 RPM. - Transfer rate: 150 MB/s. - Block size: 4 KB.

Compute the time for a random read.

???+ note "**Step 1 — rotational latency.**" One revolution: $60 / 7200 = 8.333$ ms. Average: half a revolution = **4.17 ms**. ??? info "**Step 2 — transfer time.**" $$ T_{\text{transfer}} = \frac{4096}{150 \times 10^6} \approx 0.027\ \text{ms}. $$ ??? success "**Step 3 — total.**" $$ T = 9 + 4.17 + 0.027 \approx \mathbf{13.2\ \text{ms}}. $$ **IOPS** $\approx 1 / 0.0132 \approx \mathbf{76}$. ??? tip "Sequential vs random" For sequential access, seek and rotation are amortised across many blocks. A sequential 1 GB read takes ~7 seconds (150 MB/s). A random 1 GB read takes 250,000 × 13.2 ms = **55 minutes**.

docs.title: 8.7 — Disk Scheduling: The Problem
docs.text:
The situation

The disk receives I/O requests from many processes. The order in which requests are served affects total head movement.

???+ note "The metrics" - **Total head movement** — cylinders traversed. - **Average wait time** — per request. - **Fairness** — no starvation. ???+ note "The five algorithms" | Algorithm | Description | Starvation | |---|---|---| | **FCFS** | Serve in arrival order | No | | **SSTF** | Shortest seek time first | **Yes** | | **SCAN** | Elevator — sweep in one direction | No | | **C-SCAN** | Circular SCAN — always one direction | No | | **LOOK** | SCAN but reverse at last request | No |

docs.title: Worked example 8.2 — Disk scheduling comparison
docs.text:
Problem:

Request queue: 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67. Head starts at 53.

???+ note "**FCFS** — serve in order." Path: 53 → 98 → 183 → 37 → 122 → 14 → 124 → 65 → 67. Movement: $45+85+146+85+108+110+59+2 = \mathbf{640}$. ??? info "**SSTF** — shortest seek first." Path: 53 → 65 → 67 → 37 → 14 → 98 → 122 → 124 → 183. Movement: $12+2+30+23+84+24+2+59 = \mathbf{236}$. ??? info "**SCAN (toward 0 first).**" Path: 53 → 37 → 14 → 0 → 65 → 67 → 98 → 122 → 124 → 183. Movement: $16+23+14+65+2+31+24+2+59 = \mathbf{236}$. ??? info "**C-SCAN (toward 0, wrap to 199).**" Path: 53 → 37 → 14 → 0 → 199 → 183 → 124 → 122 → 98 → 67 → 65. Movement: $16+23+14+199+16+59+2+24+31+2 = \mathbf{386}$. ??? success "**Observation.** SSTF minimises total movement (236) but is unfair — it can starve far-away requests. SCAN gives similar movement with better fairness. C-SCAN is worse on this queue but is **uniform** — every request waits about the same."

docs.title: 8.8 — The Elevator Analogy
docs.text:
SCAN as an elevator

An elevator goes up, then down, then up — never reversing mid-floor unless it has to. SCAN does the same: - Sweep in one direction, serving all requests. - Reverse at the end of the disk. - Sweep back.

???+ note "Why this works" By serving all requests in one direction before reversing, SCAN minimises the **total** seek distance. The elevator doesn't zigzag — it makes one efficient pass. ???+ tip "LOOK vs SCAN" SCAN reverses at the **edge of the disk** (cylinder 0 or maximum). LOOK reverses at the **last request** in the current direction — saving the trip to the edge if there are no requests there. LOOK is the practical choice.

docs.title: 8.9 — Buffering
docs.text:
Definition

Buffering stores data temporarily between a producer and a consumer. The OS uses buffers to absorb speed mismatches.

???+ note "Three types" | Type | Buffers | Use case | |---|---|---| | **Single** | One buffer | Simple I/O | | **Double** | Two buffers | Streaming with overlap | | **Circular** | Ring of buffers | Continuous data (network, audio) | ???+ note "Double buffering" While the producer fills buffer A, the consumer drains buffer B. When A is full and B is empty, they swap. ???+ info "Why buffering matters" - **Speed mismatch** — CPU produces 10 GB/s; disk absorbs 150 MB/s. - **Size mismatch** — network packets are 1500 bytes; file systems write 4 KB blocks. - **Copy semantics** — buffering gives a consistent snapshot even if the source changes.

docs.title: 8.10 — Caching
docs.text:
Definition

A cache stores recently used data to avoid re-fetching it.

???+ note "Buffering vs caching" | Aspect | Buffering | Caching | |---|---|---| | Purpose | Absorb mismatch | Avoid re-fetching | | Data | Data in transit | Recently used data | | Lifetime | Until consumed | Until evicted | | Example | Network buffer | Buffer cache | ???+ note "The buffer cache" The OS keeps a **page cache** of recently accessed file pages. A read that hits the cache avoids disk I/O — 100,000× faster. ???+ info "Cache coherence" Multiple caches (file system cache, disk controller cache, application cache) can disagree. **`fsync()`** forces all caches to flush — essential for durability.

docs.title: 8.11 — Spooling
docs.text:
Definition

SPOOL (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line) — queue output for a device that can only handle one job at a time.

???+ note "The classic example" 
Process A → spooler queue → printer
Process B →     │
Process C →     │
                ▼
          printed sequentially
???+ info "Where spooling is used" - **Printers** — one printer, many jobs. - **Batch processing** — job cards submitted to a queue. - **Mail servers** — outgoing messages queued before sending. !!! tip "Spooling vs buffering" Buffering is a **temporary store** during a single I/O operation. Spooling is a **persistent queue** of jobs — it survives crashes and restarts.

docs.title: 8.12 — I/O Performance Measurement
docs.text: Key metrics Metric Definition IOPS I/O operations per second Throughput Bytes per second Latency Time per operation Queue depth Outstanding requests   ???+ note "The trade-offs"     - **High IOPS** — many small transfers (databases).     - **High throughput** — large transfers (backup, video).     - **Low latency** — few outstanding requests.     ???+ info "Typical numbers"     | Device | IOPS (random 4K) | Throughput (seq) |     |---|---|---|     | HDD 7200 RPM | 75–100 | 100–200 MB/s |     | SATA SSD | 100,000 | 500 MB/s |     | NVMe SSD | 500,000+ | 3–7 GB/s |     !!! tip "IOPS matters for databases"     A relational database workload is dominated by **random 4 KB reads** (index lookups, row fetches). This is why NVMe SSDs gave 10× speedups to databases even though sequential throughput only doubled.

docs.title: Chapter 8 — key takeaways
docs.text: **1.** **I/O devices** are classified as **block**, **character**, or **network**. Each has its own access model.     **2.** The four **I/O software layers** — user library, OS-independent, drivers, interrupt handlers — separate concerns cleanly.     **3.** **Programmed I/O** busy-waits; **interrupt I/O** frees the CPU; **DMA** minimises CPU involvement for bulk transfers.     **4.** **Disk scheduling** (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK) trades **throughput** against **fairness**. SCAN and LOOK are standard.     **5.** **Buffering**, **caching**, and **spooling** absorb speed mismatches — each with a different use case.     **6.** **IOPS** and **throughput** measure different workloads. Databases care about IOPS; backup cares about throughput.

docs.title: Next — Chapter 9
docs.text:
Introduction to Security.

- **Threats**: malware (virus, worm, trojan), buffer overflow, DoS, social engineering. - **Authentication**: passwords, biometrics, MFA. - **Authorisation**: DAC, MAC, RBAC. - **Defences**: sandboxing, ASLR, DEP, firewalls, encryption. Chapters 1–8 built a working OS. Chapter 9 asks: **what can go wrong?**

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text: 1. Classify **threats**: malware, buffer overflow, DoS, social engineering.     2. Explain the **three factors** of authentication.     3. Distinguish **authentication** from **authorisation**.     4. Describe **access control models**: DAC, MAC, RBAC.     5. Explain **modern defences**: ASLR, DEP, sandboxing, encryption.

docs.title: 9.1 — Why Security?
docs.text:
The trust problem

Every system has a trust boundary. Inside the boundary, components trust each other. Across the boundary, they must not.

???+ note "Threat model" A **threat model** identifies: - What the attacker wants (data, execution, denial). - What the attacker controls (input, network, local files). - What the attacker cannot do (cross the trust boundary). !!! tip "Defence in depth" No single defence is unbreakable. Real systems combine many defences — a **layered** approach. Breaking in requires defeating **all** layers, not just one.

docs.title: 9.2 — Malware: Three Fundamental Types
docs.text:
Virus

A virus is malicious code attached to a host program. When the host runs, the virus runs.

???+ info "Virus characteristics" - **Requires user action** — running an infected program. - **Self-replicates** into other files. - **Payloads** vary — data theft, destruction, ransomware. ???+ note "Worm" A **worm** is a **standalone** malicious program that **self-propagates** over the network. ???+ info "Worm characteristics" - **Does not need a host** — runs on its own. - **Self-propagates** via network exploits. - **Very fast** — no user action needed. ???+ note "Trojan" A **trojan** is malicious code **disguised** as legitimate software. ???+ info "Trojan characteristics" - **User installs it voluntarily** — thinking it's useful. - **Does not self-replicate** — relies on the user to spread it. - **Examples:** fake antivirus, pirated software, free games. !!! warning "Worms are the most dangerous" - **Virus:** requires user action → slow spread. - **Worm:** no user action → exponential spread (minutes). - **Trojan:** requires social engineering → targeted. The **Morris worm** (1988) infected 10% of the internet in 24 hours — this is why worms are so feared. --- ## 9.3 — Buffer Overflow ???+ note "The vulnerability" A **buffer overflow** occurs when a program writes more data into a buffer than it can hold, overwriting adjacent memory. ???+ note "The classic stack overflow" 
void vulnerable(char *input) {
    char buffer[64];
    strcpy(buffer, input);   // no bounds check!
}
???+ note "The stack layout" 
┌──────────────────┐  ← higher addresses
│ return address   │  ← overwritten by overflow!
├──────────────────┤
│ saved EBP        │
├──────────────────┤
│ buffer[0..63]    │
└──────────────────┘  ← lower addresses
If `input` is longer than 64 bytes, it overwrites the saved EBP and return address. ???+ note "The attack" 1. Attacker writes a long string: 64 bytes of filler + new return address. 2. New return address points to shellcode (also in the buffer). 3. When the function returns, the CPU jumps to the attacker's code. !!! warning "Buffer overflows have dominated exploits for 30+ years" Morris worm (1988), Code Red (2001), Slammer (2003), Heartbleed (2014) — all buffer overflows. The pattern is universal; the defences have evolved, but the vulnerability remains common in C code. --- ## 9.4 — Defences Against Buffer Overflow ???+ note "Four defences" | Defence | How it works | |---|---| | **Stack canaries** | Random value between buffer and return address; checked on return | | **ASLR** | Randomise stack/heap/library addresses | | **DEP / NX** | Mark stack/heap as non-executable | | **Safe languages** | Java, Rust, Python check bounds automatically | ???+ note "Stack canaries" 
┌──────────────────┐
│ return address   │
├──────────────────┤
│ canary (random)  │  ← if it changes, crash
├──────────────────┤
│ saved EBP        │
├──────────────────┤
│ buffer           │
└──────────────────┘
The compiler inserts a random value before the return address and checks it on return. If it's changed, the program aborts. ???+ note "ASLR" **Address Space Layout Randomisation** — the OS randomises where the stack, heap, and libraries are placed. The attacker cannot predict the return address to jump to. ???+ note "DEP / NX" **Data Execution Prevention / No-eXecute** — the CPU marks memory pages as non-executable. If the attacker puts shellcode on the stack, it cannot run. !!! tip "Defence in depth" Canaries, ASLR, and DEP are **complementary**. A successful attack must bypass all three. This is why modern systems are still vulnerable — each defence is defeatable in isolation, but together they raise the bar enormously. --- ## 9.5 — Denial of Service (DoS) ???+ note "The attack" Flood a service with requests until it can no longer serve legitimate users. ???+ note "Three flavours" | Type | Description | |---|---| | **Volumetric** | Flood bandwidth (Gbps) | | **Protocol** | Exploit protocol state (SYN flood) | | **Application** | Slow HTTP requests, expensive queries | ???+ note "Distributed DoS (DDoS)" Use a **botnet** of compromised machines to attack from many sources. The target cannot simply block one IP. ???+ info "Defences" - **Rate limiting** — cap requests per IP. - **Traffic filtering** — block known-bad IPs. - **Anycast** — distribute the load across many servers. - **CDN** — absorb the traffic at the edge. - **CAPTCHAs** — distinguish humans from bots. --- ## 9.6 — Social Engineering ???+ note "The attack" Manipulate **people**, not systems, to gain access. ???+ note "Three common techniques" | Technique | Example | |---|---| | **Phishing** | Fake email from "IT" asking for password | | **Pretexting** | Call claiming to be a vendor needing access | | **Baiting** | USB drive in the parking lot | ???+ info "Why it works" Humans are not trained to detect deception. Phishing emails exploit **trust**, **urgency**, and **authority** — the same levers that legitimate communication uses. ???+ note "Defences" - **Training** — teach employees to recognise phishing. - **Verification** — call back on a known number to confirm. - **MFA** — even a stolen password is useless without the second factor. - **Restricted access** — least privilege limits the damage of a compromised account. --- ## 9.7 — Authentication: The Three Factors ???+ note "Something you know" **Passwords, PINs, security questions.** - **Pros:** familiar, cheap. - **Cons:** phishable, reusable, hard to remember securely. ???+ note "Something you have" **Smart cards, hardware tokens, phones (TOTP).** - **Pros:** not phishable directly. - **Cons:** can be lost or stolen. ???+ note "Something you are" **Fingerprints, face, iris, voice.** - **Pros:** hard to copy, always available. - **Cons:** cannot be changed if compromised. ???+ note "The strength ordering" MFA (multi-factor) > something you have > something you are > something you know. !!! tip "Passwords must be hashed, never plaintext" Store **salted hashes** (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2). Never store the password itself. Never use fast hashes (MD5, SHA-1) — they enable rainbow-table and brute-force attacks. --- ## 9.8 — Authorisation: Access Control Models ???+ note "Definition" **Authorisation** determines **what** an authenticated user can do. Authentication says "who you are"; authorisation says "what you can access". ???+ note "Three models" | Model | Description | Example | |---|---|---| | **DAC** (Discretionary) | Owner decides | Unix file permissions | | **MAC** (Mandatory) | System-wide policy | SELinux, AppArmor | | **RBAC** (Role-Based) | Roles have permissions | Enterprise systems | ???+ note "DAC — Unix permissions" 
-rwxr-xr-x  file.txt
 │││││││
 ││││││└── others: r-x
 ││││└──── group:  r-x
 │││└───── owner:  rwx
 ││└────── file type: -
 └└─────── special:  -
The owner decides who gets access. ???+ note "MAC — SELinux" Every process and file has a **security context** (user, role, type). The kernel enforces policies like: 
allow httpd_t var_log_t:file { read write };
Only httpd can read/write its log files, even if the OS user has permissions. ???+ note "RBAC — role-based" Users are assigned **roles**. Roles have **permissions**. Access is checked via the role. 
alice → doctor → read(patient_record)
bob   → nurse  → read(patient_record)
--- ## 9.9 — Encryption: At Rest and In Transit ???+ note "At rest" **Disk encryption** — full-disk (BitLocker, FileVault) or per-file. - **LUKS** (Linux) — encrypts the entire block device. - **eCryptfs** — per-file encryption in the filesystem. ???+ note "In transit" **TLS** — encrypts network traffic. - **Client → server** — negotiate cipher, exchange keys. - **Then** — symmetric encryption (AES, ChaCha20). ???+ note "The two encryption types" | Type | Speed | Use | |---|---|---| | **Symmetric** (AES) | Fast (~1 GB/s) | Bulk data | | **Asymmetric** (RSA, ECC) | Slow (~1 MB/s) | Key exchange, signatures | !!! tip "Real systems use both" TLS uses **asymmetric** to exchange a **symmetric** session key, then **symmetric** for the actual data. This gives the security of asymmetric with the speed of symmetric. --- ## 9.10 — Sandboxing ???+ note "Definition" **Sandboxing** isolates a program in a restricted environment — it can only access the resources the sandbox allows. ???+ note "Examples" - **Browser tabs** — each tab runs in a separate process with restricted permissions. - **Containers** — Docker, LXC isolate processes. - **iOS/Android apps** — each app runs in its own sandbox directory. - **seccomp** (Linux) — restricts which syscalls a process can make. ???+ info "What the sandbox controls" | Resource | How | |---|---| | **Filesystem** | Chroot, mount namespaces | | **Network** | Network namespaces, firewalls | | **CPU / memory** | Cgroups, rlimits | | **Syscalls** | seccomp filters | !!! warning "Sandboxes are not impenetrable" Escaping a container is possible (e.g., Dirty COW, runc CVE-2019-5736). A sandbox reduces the attack surface but does not eliminate it. --- ## 9.11 — Threat Modelling in Practice ???+ note "STRIDE framework" | Threat | Description | |---|---| | **Spoofing** | Pretending to be someone else | | **Tampering** | Modifying data | | **Repudiation** | Denying an action | | **Information disclosure** | Revealing private data | | **Denial of service** | Preventing access | | **Elevation of privilege** | Gaining higher access | ???+ note "Applying STRIDE to a login form" | Threat | Mitigation | |---|---| | **Spoofing** | MFA | | **Tampering** | HTTPS, CSRF tokens | | **Repudiation** | Audit logs | | **Info disclosure** | Password hashing, rate limit error messages | | **DoS** | Rate limiting, CAPTCHA | | **Privilege escalation** | Least privilege | !!! tip "The threat model is the design" Security is not a feature you add at the end — it is a **design property**. A system with a clear threat model is more secure than one that adds defences reactively. --- ## 9.12 — The Security Mindset ???+ note "Three principles" | Principle | Meaning | |---|---| | **Least privilege** | Every component has only the access it needs | | **Defence in depth** | Multiple layers of defence | | **Fail securely** | On failure, deny access (not grant) | ???+ info "The attacker's advantage" The defender must protect **every** entry point. The attacker needs to find **one** weakness. This asymmetry means security is always hard — and why **defence in depth** is essential. ???+ note "Theoretical vs practical" - **Theoretical security:** unbreakable (one-time pad, formally verified). - **Practical security:** hard enough that the cost of attack exceeds the value. Real systems are always practical — the question is how high the bar is. --- ## Chapter 9 — key takeaways **1.** **Malware**: viruses need user action, **worms self-propagate**, trojans disguise as legitimate. **2.** **Buffer overflows** overwrite adjacent memory, including return addresses. Defences: **canaries**, **ASLR**, **DEP**, safe languages. **3.** **DoS** attacks flood a service; DDoS uses a botnet. Defences: rate limiting, CDN, CAPTCHA. **4.** **Social engineering** targets humans. **Training** and **MFA** are the best defences. **5.** **Authentication** verifies identity; **authorisation** controls access. Three factors: know, have, are. **6.** **Access control**: DAC (owner), MAC (policy), RBAC (roles). **7.** **Encryption**: symmetric for speed, asymmetric for key exchange. **TLS** combines both. **8.** **Sandboxing** isolates programs. **Least privilege**, **defence in depth**, **fail securely** are the guiding principles. --- ## Course wrap-up **The arc of ECEG-5202:** 1. **Chapter 1** — what an OS is, and why it exists. 2. **Chapter 2** — processes and threads. 3. **Chapter 3** — CPU scheduling. 4. **Chapter 4** — synchronization and IPC. 5. **Chapter 5** — deadlocks. 6. **Chapter 6** — memory management. 7. **Chapter 7** — file systems. 8. **Chapter 8** — I/O management. 9. **Chapter 9** — security. !!! tip "The unifying question" Every chapter asked: **how does the OS multiplex a finite resource across many processes, safely and efficiently?** - **CPU** — scheduling. - **Memory** — paging and virtual memory. - **Disk** — file systems and I/O scheduling. - **Shared data** — synchronisation and deadlock avoidance. - **Access** — security. **Good luck with the exam.**

docs.title: C1 — Minimum average waiting time [2]
docs.text:
Answer: (b) SJF.

SJF provably minimises average waiting time because at every step it picks the job that will finish soonest, leaving the smallest possible residual waiting time for the rest. The exchange argument: swapping a longer job ahead of a shorter one can only increase the total wait.

docs.title: C2 — RR with very large quantum [2]
docs.text:
Answer: (b) FCFS.

If the quantum exceeds every burst time, no process is ever preempted; each runs to completion in arrival order — exactly FCFS.

docs.title: C3 — Average waiting time under FCFS, SJF, RR (q = 2) [4]
docs.text:
Given: five processes, all arriving at time 0, burst times 10, 2, 4, 6, 8.

FCFS. Order P1, P2, P3, P4, P5. Waits: 0, 10, 12, 16, 22. Average = 12.0.

SJF. Order P2, P3, P4, P5, P1. Waits: 0, 2, 6, 12, 20. Average = 8.0.

RR (q = 2). Trace the queue. Average ≈ 11.6 (full trace in the chapter's worked example 3.1).

docs.title: C4 — Priority inversion [4]
docs.text:
Problem. A high-priority task \(H\) waits for a lock held by a low-priority task \(L\); a medium-priority task \(M\) preempts \(L\), delaying \(H\) indefinitely.

Fix — priority inheritance. While \(L\) holds a lock that \(H\) is waiting for, \(L\)'s priority is temporarily raised to \(H\)'s. \(M\) can no longer preempt \(L\); \(L\) finishes and releases the lock; \(H\) proceeds.

Example where it matters. The 1997 Mars Pathfinder mission experienced repeated reboots due to priority inversion in the VxWorks scheduler; the fix was enabling priority inheritance.
